I'll bring Thrasymachus's argument back to life. First, I'll explain what people say justice is and where it comes from. Second, I'll argue that everyone who practices it does so unwillingly, as something they have to do, not as something good. And third, I'll show why that view makes sense, because the life of the unjust man is, they say, far better than the life of the just. I don't actually believe any of this myself, Socrates. But my ears are full of Thrasymachus and a thousand others, and I've never once heard anyone defend justice, and show that it beats injustice, in a way that satisfied me. I want to hear justice praised for what it is in itself, and you're the man I most expect to hear it from. So I'll throw everything I have into praising the unjust life, and the way I argue will show you exactly the way I want to hear you argue back, praising justice and condemning injustice. Will you let me try it like that?'
'Nothing could please me more,' I said. 'It's the kind of subject a sensible man would want to talk about again and again.'
'Good,' he said. 'Then listen, while I keep to my plan and start with the nature and origin of justice.'

'People say that doing wrong is by nature a good thing and suffering wrong a bad thing, but that the harm of suffering it outweighs the good of doing it. So once men have tried both, once they've done wrong and been wronged in turn, those who can't manage to grab the one and dodge the other decide it pays to make an agreement: no one does wrong, and no one suffers it. That's where laws and contracts come from, and people call what the law commands lawful and just. This, they say, is the origin of justice and what it really is. It stands midway between the best case, doing wrong and getting away with it, and the worst case, being wronged with no power to strike back. Justice sits between these two, and people put up with it, not because it's good, but as the lesser evil, prized only because they're too weak to do wrong with impunity. No real man, no one with the power to do wrong, would ever make such a bargain. He'd be mad to. That, Socrates, is the standard account of what justice is and where it comes from.'

'And the proof that people act justly only under compulsion, because they lack the power to do wrong, comes through most clearly if we try a thought-experiment. Give both the just man and the unjust man the freedom to do whatever they please, and then follow them and watch where their desires lead. We'll catch the just man red-handed, heading down the very same road as the unjust one, driven by the appetite to have more, which every nature pursues as its good, though law forces it back into line and makes it respect equality. The clearest way to give them this freedom would be to grant them the power that once belonged, so the story goes, to Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus the Lydian. Gyges was a shepherd in the service of the Lydian king. One day there was a great storm, and an earthquake split open the ground where he was pasturing his flock. Amazed, he climbed down into the chasm, and there, among other wonders, he saw a hollow bronze horse with little doors in its side. Stooping to look inside, he saw a corpse, larger than human, it seemed, wearing nothing but a gold ring on its hand. He slipped the ring off and climbed back out. Now, the shepherds held their usual monthly meeting to send the king a report on the flocks, and Gyges came wearing the ring. As he sat among the others, he happened to turn the setting of the ring toward the inside of his hand, and at once he became invisible, and the others started talking about him as though he'd left. Astonished, he fingered the ring again, turned the setting back outward, and reappeared. He tested it again and again, and the result was always the same: setting turned in, he vanished; turned out, he reappeared. As soon as he was sure of this, he arranged to be one of the messengers sent to the king. Once at court, he seduced the queen, plotted with her against the king, killed him, and seized the throne. Now suppose there were two such rings, and the just man put on one and the unjust man the other. No one, it seems, would be made of iron enough to stay on the path of justice and keep his hands off other people's things when he could take whatever he wanted from the market stalls without being seen, walk into any house and sleep with anyone he liked, kill or free whomever he chose, and in every way act like a god among men. The two of them would end up behaving exactly alike, both walking the same road. And surely this is strong evidence that no one is just willingly, but only under compulsion, because no one believes justice is any good to him personally. The moment a man thinks he can get away with doing wrong, he does it. Everyone, deep down, believes that injustice pays far better than justice, and on this account they're right to believe it. If a man got hold of such a power and then never once used it to do wrong or to lay a hand on what wasn't his, anyone watching would think him utterly pathetic, an idiot, though of course they'd praise him to his face, lying to one another out of their own fear of being wronged. So much for that.'

'Now, if we're going to judge between the lives of the just and the unjust man, we have to set each of them apart in his pure form. There's no other way to do it. And how do we manage that? Like this. We strip nothing away from the unjust man's injustice or the just man's justice. We make each of them perfect in his own line of work. First, the unjust man. Let him operate like a real master of his craft. A top pilot or doctor knows exactly what his skill can and can't do; he attempts what's within his reach and, if he slips, he can recover. So let the unjust man commit his crimes the right way, and stay hidden if he means to be great at injustice, because the man who gets caught is a bungler. The highest reach of injustice is to seem just while being the opposite. So we must grant our perfectly unjust man his perfect injustice, taking nothing away: while committing the worst crimes, he has secured for himself the finest reputation for justice. If he ever stumbles, he can set himself right; he's persuasive enough to talk his way clear if any of his deeds come to light, and forceful enough to get his way where force is needed, backed by his courage, his strength, his money, and his friends. Now set beside him the just man, plain and noble, who wants, in Aeschylus's words, not to seem good but to be it. So we have to take away the seeming. If he seems just, he'll get honors and rewards for it, and then we won't be able to tell whether he's just for justice's sake or for the sake of the rewards. Strip him bare, then, of everything but his justice, and put him in the opposite situation from the other man. Though he does no wrong, give him the worst reputation for wrongdoing, so that his justice is put to the ultimate test and we can see whether it bends under disgrace and all that disgrace brings. Let him hold his course, unchanging, to his dying breath, being just while seeming unjust his whole life long. Then, when both have reached the very limit, one of justice and the other of injustice, let us decide which of them is the happier.'
'Good heavens, Glaucon,' I said, 'how vigorously you scrub the two of them down for judgment, like a man polishing a pair of statues!'

'I'm doing my best,' he said. 'And now that we know what each of them is like, there's no trouble describing the life that awaits them. Let me do it, then. And if what I say sounds harsh, Socrates, remember that the words aren't mine. Put them in the mouths of the men who praise injustice. They'll tell you that the just man, with his reputation for wrongdoing, will be whipped, racked, and chained; they'll burn out his eyes; and in the end, after suffering every torment, he'll be impaled. Then he'll learn that one should want not to be just but to seem so. In fact, Aeschylus's line fits the unjust man far better than the just: it's the unjust man who pursues reality, who lives for what truly is and not for appearances. He wants to be unjust, not merely seem it.'
'"Deep is the soil of his mind, and from it / the harvest of his shrewd designs springs up."'

'First, because he's thought to be just, he holds office in the city. He can marry into any family he likes and give his own children in marriage where he pleases. He can do business and form partnerships with anyone, and since he has no scruples about doing wrong, he comes out ahead in every dealing and grows rich. He helps his friends and harms his enemies. He makes lavish, magnificent sacrifices and offerings to the gods, and serves them, and serves any man he wishes to honor, far better than the just man can, so it's likely the gods will love him more than the just man too. And so, Socrates, men say, and the gods agree, that a better life is laid up for the unjust man than for the just.'
I was about to answer Glaucon when his brother Adeimantus broke in. 'Surely you don't think the case has been fully made, Socrates?'
'Why, what's left?' I said.
'The single most important point hasn't even been mentioned,' he said.

'Well,' I said, 'as the proverb has it, let a man's brother stand by him. So if Glaucon has left anything out, you come to his aid, though I have to admit he's already floored me as it is, and left me no strength to defend justice.'

'That's nonsense,' he said. 'But hear me out, because there's another side to Glaucon's argument that needs saying if we're to bring out his full meaning. When fathers tell their sons to be just, and tutors tell their charges the same, what is it they praise? Not justice itself, but the good name it brings. They want the boy, by being thought just, to land the offices and marriages and all the rest of the advantages that Glaucon listed as flowing from a reputation for justice. In fact these people pile even more onto the rewards of reputation. They throw in the favor of the gods, and they'll tell you of the showers of blessings the heavens rain down on the pious, just as the good Hesiod and Homer say. Hesiod says the gods make the oaks of the just'
'"bear acorns at the top and bees in the middle, / and their woolly sheep stagger under the weight of their fleeces,"'
'and many other blessings of the kind. Homer says much the same, speaking of a man whose fame is'

'"like the fame of a blameless king who, godlike, / upholds justice, and the black earth bears him / wheat and barley, his trees are heavy with fruit, / his flocks bring forth without fail, and the sea yields him fish."'

'And Musaeus and his son promise the just even grander gifts from the gods. In their telling, they bring the just down to the next world, lay them on couches, set a feast going, and crown them with garlands, so that they spend all eternity drunk, as though everlasting drunkenness were virtue's finest reward. Others stretch the rewards still further: the children and grandchildren of the pious and just, they say, will survive to the third and fourth generation. That's how they praise justice. But the wicked they bury in mud down in Hades and set to carrying water in a sieve; and while these men are still alive, they drag their names through the dirt, and load on them all the punishments Glaucon described as falling to the just man who's thought unjust. That's the whole of their repertoire. So that's how the one is praised and the other condemned.'

'And now, Socrates, here's yet another way of talking about justice and injustice, one you find not only in the poets but in ordinary speech. With one voice everyone keeps saying that justice and self-control are admirable, yes, but hard and full of toil, while loose living and injustice are sweet and easy to come by, and only convention and reputation hold them to be shameful. They say injustice usually pays better than justice, and they're perfectly willing to call wicked men happy, and to honor them in public and private, so long as they're rich or otherwise powerful, while they look down on and ignore the weak and poor, even while admitting these are the better men. But the strangest thing of all is what they say about the gods and goodness. They claim the gods hand out hardship and misery to many good men, and the opposite lot to their opposites. And then there are the begging priests and fortune-tellers who knock on rich men's doors and convince them that the gods have given them a power, worked through sacrifices and spells amid feasting and festivity, to absolve any wrong the man or his ancestors have done; and that if he wants to ruin some enemy, just or unjust, a small fee will do it, since with their incantations and binding spells they can press the gods into their service. And for all of this they call the poets to witness. Some smooth the path of vice by quoting Hesiod:'
'"Wickedness is easy to get in plenty: the road is smooth and she lives close by. / But in front of virtue the gods have set sweat,"'
'and a long, steep, uphill road. Others cite Homer to prove that the gods can be swayed by men, since he too says:'
'"The gods themselves can be moved. With sacrifices and gentle prayers, / with offerings and the savor of burnt fat, men turn them aside / when they have transgressed and done wrong."'

'And they produce a heap of books by Musaeus and Orpheus, children of the Moon and the Muses, so they claim, and they conduct their rituals from them. They persuade not only individuals but whole cities that there are absolutions and purifications for wrongdoing, available to the living through sacrifices and pleasant games, and available to the dead too, through what they call initiations, which release us from the torments of the next world, while those who skip them, they warn, face horrors no one can name.'

'Now, my dear Socrates,' he went on, 'when the young hear all of this said about goodness and badness, and how gods and men regard them, what do you suppose it does to them, especially the quick-witted ones, who flit like bees from one of these sayings to the next and try to work out from all of it what sort of person to be and which road to take to make the most of life? Such a youth will surely ask himself, in Pindar's words,'
'"Shall I climb to the higher rampart by justice, / or by crooked deceit, and so fortify myself for life?"'

'What they tell me is this. If I'm really just but don't seem so, there's no profit in it, only pain and loss, by all accounts. But if I'm unjust and yet build up a reputation for justice, a heavenly life is promised me. Very well: since the wise tell me that the look of a thing overpowers the truth of it and is the master of happiness, that's clearly where I must turn. I'll paint a front of virtue around myself, a facade for show, but behind it I'll trail the cunning, twisting fox of Archilochus. "But it's hard," someone objects, "to keep wickedness hidden forever." Nothing great is easy, I answer. Still, if happiness is the goal, this is plainly the road the argument points to. To stay hidden we'll form secret societies and political clubs; and there are teachers of persuasion who pass on the skills of the law courts and the assembly. So, partly by persuasion and partly by force, I'll get the better of others and not be punished. "But you can't outwit or overpower the gods." Well, suppose there are no gods, or suppose they take no interest in human affairs. Then why should we care about staying hidden from them? And if the gods do exist and do care, we know of them only from tradition and from the poets who trace their family trees, and these are the very people who say the gods can be swayed and turned aside by sacrifices, gentle prayers, and offerings. We should believe them on both points or neither. If we believe them, then the thing to do is commit injustice and offer up sacrifices from the proceeds. If we're just, we'll only escape punishment by the gods while forfeiting the profits of injustice; but if we're unjust, we'll keep the profits and, by praying as we sin and sinning as we pray, we'll talk the gods round and get off free. "But in the world below we'll pay, we or our descendants, for the wrongs we do here." My friend, the youth will reason, that's what the initiations and the absolving gods are for, and they have great power. The greatest cities tell us so, and so do the children of the gods, the poets and prophets, who say the same.'

'So on what grounds would we still choose justice over the worst injustice, when, if we wrap that injustice in a convincing show of virtue, we'll do exactly as we please with gods and men, in this life and the next, as the most numerous and the highest authorities assure us? Given all this, Socrates, how could any man with some advantage of mind, looks, birth, or wealth bring himself to honor justice, instead of laughing out loud whenever he hears it praised? Even a man who could prove what I'm saying false, and who is convinced that justice is best, feels no anger at the unjust; he forgives them readily, because he knows that no one is just willingly, unless some god-given disgust at injustice holds him back, or he's come to know the truth. Apart from such a man, no one is just by choice. It's only cowardice or old age or some other weakness that makes a man condemn injustice, namely, his own inability to commit it, as is shown by the fact that the moment he gets the power, he uses it to do wrong as much as he can.'

'And the root of all this, Socrates, is the very thing my brother and I told you at the start, when we said how astonished we were that, of all of you who profess to champion justice, from the ancient heroes whose words survive down to the men of today, not one has ever condemned injustice or praised justice except in terms of the reputations, honors, and rewards that come of them. What none of you has ever done, in verse or in prose, is to describe what each of them, by its own power, does within the soul of its possessor, unseen by any eye, god's or man's; to show that injustice is the greatest of all the evils a soul can carry inside it, and justice the greatest good. If you had all said this from the beginning, and persuaded us of it from childhood, we wouldn't be standing guard over one another to prevent wrongdoing. Each man would be his own best guard, terrified that by doing wrong he'd be taking the greatest of evils to live inside him. Thrasymachus, or anyone else, might say all this and more about justice and injustice, crudely turning their true natures upside down, as I think. But I've put it so forcefully, and I'll be honest with you, precisely because I want to hear you argue the other side. So don't just show us that justice is stronger than injustice. Show us what each of them does to the man who has it, in himself, that makes the one a good and the other an evil. And do as Glaucon asked: leave reputations out of it. Because if you don't strip each man of his true reputation and saddle him with a false one, we'll say you're praising not justice but the appearance of justice, and not condemning injustice but only the appearance of it; we'll conclude you're really telling us to be unjust on the sly, and that you secretly agree with Thrasymachus that justice is someone else's good, the advantage of the stronger, while injustice is a man's own profit and gain, at the weaker man's expense. You've granted that justice belongs in the highest class of goods, the ones worth having for their results but far more for themselves, like sight, hearing, understanding, health, and every other good that's genuinely good by its own nature and not merely by convention. So praise that side of justice, the good it does the man who has it just by being in him, and let others praise the wages and the reputation. From other men I'd accept that kind of praise, but not from you, who've spent your whole life on this single question. Don't just prove to us that justice beats injustice. Show us what each does to its possessor, unseen by gods or men, that makes the one good and the other evil.'

I had always admired the natural gifts of Glaucon and Adeimantus, but hearing them now, I was delighted, and I said, 'Sons of a distinguished father, the man who admired Glaucon made a fitting start to his verses when, after the two of you had won glory at the battle of Megara, he wrote:'
'"Sons of Ariston, divine offspring of a famous man."'

'The epithet fits, my friends. There's something truly godlike in your being able to argue so well for the superiority of injustice and yet remain unconvinced by your own case. And I do believe you're unconvinced. I judge that from the rest of your characters; from the speeches alone I'd have had my doubts. But the more I trust you, the harder I find it to know what to say. I can't see how I'm to defend justice. I feel I'm not up to it, and the proof of that is that you weren't satisfied with the answer I gave Thrasymachus, where I thought I'd shown justice better than injustice. Yet I can't refuse my help, not while there's breath in me and a voice to speak with. I'm afraid it would be a kind of impiety to stand by while justice is slandered and not come to her defense as long as I'm able to draw breath. So I'd better defend her as best I can.'

Glaucon and the others begged me not to let the question drop, but to press on with the inquiry, to get at the truth about what justice and injustice each are, and about their relative advantages. So I told them what I really thought. 'This inquiry we're undertaking is no light one,' I said. 'It needs sharp eyes, and since we're not especially clever, I think we should go about it the way you'd ask someone short-sighted to read small letters from far off. If someone realized the same letters appeared elsewhere in a larger size on a larger surface, it would be a godsend to read the big ones first and then check the small against them.'
'No doubt,' said Adeimantus. 'But what's the parallel to our inquiry into justice?'
'I'll tell you,' I said. 'We speak of justice as belonging to a single man, and also as belonging to a whole city, don't we?'
'We do,' he said.
'And a city is larger than one man?'
'It is.'

'Then maybe there's more justice in the larger thing, and it's easier to make out there. So if you agree, let's first look for justice in a city, and afterward look for it in the individual, comparing the smaller likeness to the larger.'
'That's an excellent idea,' he said.
'And if we watched a city coming into being in our discussion,' I said, 'we'd see its justice and its injustice coming into being too?'
'Probably,' he said.
'And once that's done, we can hope to find what we're after more easily?'
'Yes, far more easily.'
'Then should we try to carry it through? It's no small task, I think, so consider it carefully.'
'We have considered it,' said Adeimantus. 'Go ahead.'
'Well then,' I said, 'a city comes into being, I think, because none of us is self-sufficient; we each need many things. Can you think of any other reason a city gets founded?'
'No,' he said, 'none.'

'So because we have many needs, and one man calls in a second to meet one need and a third to meet another, a crowd of people gather in one place as partners and helpers, and we give this settlement the name "city." Right?'
'Yes.'
'And one man shares with another, giving and taking, because each thinks the exchange is better for himself?'
'Just so.'
'Then come,' I said, 'let's build our city from the beginning, in our discussion. Though its real builder, it seems, will be our need.'
'Of course.'
'Now the first and greatest of our needs is food, since without it there's no living and no being alive at all.'
'Certainly.'
'The second is shelter, and the third clothing and the like.'
'True.'
'Now, how will our city manage to supply all this? Won't one man be a farmer, another a builder, another a weaver? And should we add a shoemaker, or someone else to look after our bodily needs?'
'Yes.'
'So the most basic city would consist of four or five men.'
'It seems so.'

'And what then? Should each of them throw the product of his work into a common pool, the farmer, say, producing enough food for four and spending four times the labor and time growing it, to share with the others? Or should he ignore the rest, grow only a quarter of the food in a quarter of the time, and use the other three quarters to build himself a house, make his own clothes, make his own shoes, never bothering to share with anyone but supplying all his own needs himself?'
Adeimantus said, 'The first way, I'd think, Socrates. He should produce only food.'
'And that's probably the better way,' I said. 'Hearing you say it reminds me that we're not all born alike. We differ in our natures, and different natures suit different kinds of work.'
'True.'
'And is a job done better when one man works at many trades or when he sticks to one?'
'When he sticks to one.'
'And surely it's clear too that work is spoiled if you let the right moment for it pass?'
'Clearly.'
'Because the work won't wait around for the worker to have spare time. The worker has to keep at it as his main business, not treat it as a sideline.'
'He must.'

'So the conclusion is that more of everything is produced, and produced better and more easily, when each man does the one thing he's suited to by nature, does it at the right time, and leaves the other trades alone.'
'Absolutely.'

'Then we'll need more than four citizens, Adeimantus. The farmer, if he wants a decent plow and hoe and the rest of his tools, won't make them himself. Neither will the builder, who needs plenty of tools of his own. And the same for the weaver and the shoemaker.'
'True.'
'So carpenters and smiths and a whole crowd of such craftsmen will join our little settlement and make it bigger.'
'They will.'

'Still, it won't be a huge place even if we add cowherds and shepherds and the other herdsmen, so that the farmers have oxen for plowing, the builders have draft animals to haul with, and the weavers and shoemakers have fleeces and hides.'
'Yet it won't be a small city either,' he said, 'once it holds all of them.'
'And then there's the question of location,' I said. 'It's nearly impossible to set up a city where it needs to import nothing.'
'Impossible.'
'So we'll need still another set of people to fetch from other cities what ours lacks.'
'We will.'
'But if our agent shows up empty-handed, with nothing the other city wants, he'll come home empty-handed too.'
'That's right.'
'So our people must produce at home not only enough for themselves but enough, in kind and quantity, to satisfy the people they're getting things from.'
'They must.'
'So we'll need more farmers and more craftsmen in our city.'
'Yes.'
'And other agents besides, to handle the importing and exporting. These are the merchants, aren't they?'
'Yes.'
'So we'll need merchants too.'
'Certainly.'
'And if the trade goes by sea, we'll need a good many more people skilled in seafaring.'
'A good many.'
'Now, within the city itself, how will people exchange what each produces? That, after all, was our whole reason for forming a partnership and founding a city in the first place.'
'Plainly they'll buy and sell.'
'Then we'll need a marketplace and a currency, a token, for exchange.'
'Certainly.'
'Now suppose a farmer, or some other producer, brings his goods to market, but arrives when there's no one there to trade with him. Is he to sit idle in the marketplace, away from his own work?'

'Not at all,' he said. 'There are people who notice this and step in to serve as middlemen. In well-run cities these are usually the ones too weak in body to do anything else. Their job is to wait in the market, take money from those who want to buy, and hand over money to those who want to sell.'
'So this need creates a class of shopkeepers in our city. Don't we call the ones who sit in the market buying and selling shopkeepers, and the ones who travel between cities merchants?'
'Yes.'

'And there's still another class, I think, of people who aren't much as partners in thought, but who have the bodily strength for heavy work. They sell the use of their strength, and since they're paid a wage, or hire, for it, we call them hired laborers, don't we?'
'True.'
'So hired laborers help fill out the city too.'
'They do.'
'Then, Adeimantus, has our city grown to its full size now? Is it complete?'
'Perhaps so.'
'Then where in it is justice, and where injustice? Along with which of the parts we've described did they come in?'
'I can't see it, Socrates,' he said, 'unless it's somewhere in the dealings these people have with one another.'
'You may well be right,' I said. 'Let's look into it and not give up.'

'First, then, let's think about how people will live in the city we've set up. Won't they produce grain and wine and clothes and shoes, and build themselves houses? In summer they'll mostly work stripped and barefoot, and in winter they'll be well clothed and shod. They'll live on barley meal and wheat flour, kneading and baking it into fine cakes and loaves, which they'll lay out on a mat of reeds or on clean leaves. They'll stretch out on couches strewn with bryony and myrtle, and feast with their children, drinking the wine they've made, wearing garlands and singing the praises of the gods, enjoying one another's company. And they'll be careful not to have more children than they can afford, keeping an eye on poverty and on war.'
Here Glaucon broke in. 'It seems,' he said, 'you give your men a feast with no cooked dishes.'

'You're right,' I said. 'I forgot they'll have something to go with their bread, salt, of course, and olives and cheese, and they'll boil up the kinds of roots and greens you get in the country. For dessert we'll set out figs, chickpeas, and beans, and they'll roast myrtle berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation as they go. And living like this, in peace and good health, they'll most likely reach old age and pass a life of the same kind on to their children.'
'Socrates,' he said, 'if you were founding a city of pigs, isn't this exactly the fodder you'd feed them?'
'Then how should they live, Glaucon?' I asked.
'In the usual comfort,' he said. 'They should recline on proper couches, I'd think, and eat off tables, and have the sauces and sweets people have nowadays.'

'I see,' I said. 'So it's not just a city we're examining now, but a luxurious one. Well, there may be no harm in that. By looking at such a city we may all the sooner spot where justice and injustice take root in a community. The true city, the healthy one, is the one I described. But if you'd like, let's look at a fevered city too. Plenty of people, it seems, won't be content with the simple fare and the way of life I laid out. They'll want couches and tables and other furniture added, and fancy dishes, and perfumes and incense, and call girls and pastries, every kind of each. And we can't restrict ourselves any longer to the bare necessities I started with, the houses and clothes and shoes. We'll have to set painting and embroidery going, and get hold of gold and ivory and all the rest.'
'True,' he said.

'So we'll have to enlarge the city, because the healthy one isn't big enough now. We have to swell it with a whole crowd and a great mass of people who aren't there to meet any real need: hunters of every kind, and imitators, droves of them, some working with shapes and colors, others with music, poets and their assistants, reciters, actors, dancers, producers, and makers of all sorts of goods, including the ones for women's adornment. And we'll need more servants too. Don't you think we'll want attendants for boys, wet nurses and dry nurses, hairdressers, barbers, and cooks and butchers besides? And we'll need swineherds as well. There were none in our earlier city, which didn't need them, but this one will. And it will need vast herds of other animals, if people are going to eat them, won't it?'
'Of course.'
'And living this way, we'll need far more doctors than before, won't we?'
'Far more.'
'And the land that was enough to feed the original population will now be too small. Wouldn't you say so?'
'Yes.'

'So we'll have to carve off a piece of our neighbors' land if we mean to have enough to pasture and plow, and they'll want a piece of ours, if they too have given themselves over to grabbing endless wealth, past the limit of what they really need.'
'That's bound to happen, Socrates.'
'So the next step is war, Glaucon. Isn't it?'
'It is,' he said.

'We needn't yet say whether war does good or harm,' I said. 'But we can say this much: we've found the origin of war, and it lies in the very things that breed nearly all the evils a city suffers, in private and in public alike.'
'Yes.'

'So the city must grow larger again, my friend, and not by a little but by a whole army, which has to march out and fight any attackers in defense of all the city's wealth and the people we were just describing.'
'Why?' he said. 'Can't the citizens defend themselves?'
'No,' I said, 'not if the principle we all agreed on when we were founding the city was right. We agreed, you'll remember, that one man can't do many crafts well.'
'True,' he said.
'Well, isn't fighting a war a craft?'
'Very much so.'
'And should we care more about the craft of shoemaking than the craft of war?'
'Not at all.'

'Now, we wouldn't let the shoemaker try to be a farmer or a weaver or a builder at the same time. We kept him to shoemaking so that the work would be done well. We assigned each man the single trade he was suited to by nature, and had him work at that one thing his whole life, leaving the others, so as not to miss the right moments and to do good work. And surely nothing matters more than that the work of war be done well. Or is soldiering so easy a craft that a man can be a farmer or a shoemaker or a tradesman and a soldier on the side, when no one can become even a decent checkers or dice player by picking it up casually and not practicing it from childhood? Can a man pick up a shield, or any other weapon or tool of war, and become a competent fighter in the heavy infantry, or any other unit, that very same day? No other tool makes a craftsman or a champion of the man who takes it up without knowledge of it and without practice.'
'If it did,' he said, 'tools would be worth a great deal.'
'So the higher the guardians' task is, the more it will demand of them, more freedom from other work, and more skill and care than anything else.'
'I should think so.'
'And won't it demand a nature suited to that very calling?'
'Of course.'
'Then our job, it seems, is to pick out, if we can, which natures are fit for guarding the city.'
'Yes, that's our job.'
'By Zeus,' I said, 'it's no light task we've taken on. Still, we mustn't lose our nerve. We have to do the best we can.'
'We do.'
'Now,' I said, 'don't you think that, for the purpose of guarding, the nature of a well-bred young dog and a noble young man are alike?'
'What do you mean?'
'I mean that each of them must be keen-sighted, quick to spot an enemy, fast enough to chase him down once spotted, and strong enough to fight him if he has to give battle.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they need all of that.'
'And brave, if he's to fight well.'
'Of course.'

'But will any creature, horse or dog or whatever, be brave if it has no spirit? Haven't you noticed how irresistible and unbeatable spirit is, how its presence makes a soul utterly fearless and proof against everything?'
'I have.'
'So much, then, for the bodily qualities our guardian needs.'
'Yes.'
'And as for the qualities of soul, he must be full of spirit.'
'That too.'
'But, Glaucon,' I said, 'won't natures like that be fierce toward one another and toward everyone else, if that's what they're like?'
'That,' he said, 'will be hard to deal with.'
'And yet they have to be gentle to their own people and dangerous to the enemy. Otherwise they won't wait for an enemy to destroy them; they'll do it to themselves first.'
'True,' he said.
'So what are we to do?' I said. 'Where will we find a nature that's gentle and high-spirited at once, when the two seem to be opposites?'
'I don't know.'
'And yet without both of these he can't be a good guardian. So it looks impossible, and we seem forced to conclude that a good guardian can't exist.'
'I'm afraid so,' he said.
I was stuck, but turning the thing over in my mind, I said, 'We deserve to be stuck, my friend, because we've let go of the comparison we set up.'
'How so?'
'We've overlooked the fact that there really are natures with these opposite qualities together.'
'And where?'

'In several animals,' I said, 'but you can see it in the one we compared our guardian to. You know, surely, that a well-bred dog is by nature as gentle as can be with the people it knows and the opposite with strangers.'
'I do know that.'
'So it's not impossible after all. We're not asking anything against nature in looking for a guardian like that.'
'It seems not.'
'And don't you think the guardian's nature needs something more, on top of being spirited? It needs to be philosophical, a lover of wisdom.'
'How do you mean? I don't follow.'
'This too,' I said, 'you'll notice in dogs, and it's a thing worth wondering at in the animal.'
'What thing?'

'When a dog sees a stranger, it turns angry, though the man has done it no harm; and when it sees someone familiar, it greets him warmly, though he's never done it any good. Did you never find that remarkable?'
'I never really thought about it before,' he said, 'but yes, that's plainly what a dog does.'
'Well, it's a fine trait in the dog, and a truly philosophical one.'
'How so?'

'Because the dog tells friend from enemy by nothing but this: it knows the one and doesn't know the other. And how could a creature that draws the line between what's its own and what's alien by knowledge and ignorance be anything but a lover of learning?'
'It couldn't,' he said.
'And isn't loving learning the same as loving wisdom, the same as being philosophical?'
'It is.'
'So shall we say with confidence that for a man too, if he's to be gentle toward his own people and those he knows, he must by nature be a lover of wisdom and of learning?'
'Yes,' he said.
'Then the man who's going to be a truly fine and good guardian of our city will be philosophical, spirited, fast, and strong, all at once.'
'Absolutely,' he said.

'So that's what he'll be like to begin with. But how are these men to be raised and educated? And does looking into that help us with the larger question we set out to answer, namely, how justice and injustice arise in a city? We don't want to leave anything important out, but we don't want to drag the discussion out endlessly either.'
Adeimantus said, 'I certainly expect the inquiry into education to help with that.'
'Then by all means, my dear Adeimantus,' I said, 'we mustn't drop it, even if it turns out to be a bit long.'
'No, we mustn't.'
'Come, then, and let's educate these men in our discussion, as if we were telling a story at our leisure.'
'Let's do it.'
'What will their education be? It's hard to find anything better than what tradition has already worked out: physical training for the body, and the arts, music and poetry, for the soul.'
'True.'
'And shall we start with the arts, before we get to physical training?'
'Of course.'
'And when you say "the arts," do you include stories and literature, or not?'
'I do.'
'And there are two kinds of these, the true and the false?'
'Yes.'
'And our education should use both, beginning with the false?'
'I don't understand what you mean,' he said.

'Don't you see,' I said, 'that the first thing we do with children is tell them stories? And these are, on the whole, false, though there's some truth in them too. And we tell children stories before we put them to physical training.'
'That's so.'
'That's what I meant by starting with the arts before physical training.'
'You're right,' he said.

'Now, you know that in any undertaking the most important part is the beginning, especially with anything young and tender. That's when it's most malleable, and takes whatever stamp you want to impress on it.'
'Quite so.'

'Then shall we casually let children hear just any stories, made up by just anyone, and take into their souls beliefs that are mostly the opposite of the ones we think they should hold when they grow up?'
'We certainly won't allow that.'

'So our first job, it seems, is to supervise the storytellers. We'll approve the good stories they tell and reject the bad ones, and we'll have the mothers and nurses tell the children only the approved ones, and shape their souls with these stories far more than they shape their bodies with their hands. But most of the stories they now tell will have to be thrown out.'
'Which ones?' he asked.
'If we look at the great stories,' I said, 'we'll see the pattern of the small ones too, since great and small are bound to share the same type and have the same effect. Don't you think so?'
'I do,' he said. 'But I don't even know which you mean by the great stories.'
'The ones Homer and Hesiod told us,' I said, 'and the other poets. They've always been the great storytellers of mankind, telling the tales men still tell.'
'Which stories do you mean,' he said, 'and what fault do you find with them?'
'The fault one should mind most of all,' I said, 'especially when the lie is an ugly one.'
'And what's that?'
'Misrepresenting, in speech, what the gods and heroes are really like, the way a painter paints a portrait with no likeness at all to what he meant to paint.'
'Yes,' he said, 'we're right to object to that. But which stories do you mean exactly?'

'First of all,' I said, 'the biggest lie about the most important things, the one whose teller told it badly: how Uranus did the things Hesiod says he did, and how Cronus took his revenge on him. As for the deeds of Cronus, and what his son in turn did to him, even if they were true I'd say they shouldn't be told so lightly to the young and foolish. Better to keep silent. But if there were some need to tell them, only a tiny few should hear them in secret, after sacrificing not an ordinary piglet but some huge victim almost no one could afford, so that as few people as possible would ever hear them.'
'Yes,' he said, 'those stories are indeed hard to defend.'

'And they shouldn't be told in our city, Adeimantus,' I said. 'A young man mustn't be told that in committing the worst of crimes he's doing nothing out of the ordinary, nor that if he punishes a father who's done wrong, by any means whatever, he's only doing what the first and greatest of the gods did.'
'No,' he said, 'I quite agree those tales aren't fit to be repeated.'

'Nor should we have any talk at all of gods warring on gods, plotting against them, and fighting them, none of it true, if we mean the future guardians of our city to think that turning on one another is the most shameful thing there is. Far less should we tell them, or have them embroidered on tapestries, the battles of the giants and all the many other feuds the gods and heroes had with their own kin and kindred. If we mean to convince them that no two citizens have ever quarreled and that to quarrel is unholy, then that's the sort of thing the old men and women should tell the children from the start, and the poets must be compelled to compose in the same spirit once the children are older. As for the tale of Hephaestus being chained up by his mother Hera, or Hephaestus flung out of heaven by his father for trying to defend his mother when she was being beaten, and all the battles of the gods that Homer has composed, we mustn't admit them into the city, whether they're written with a hidden meaning or without one. A young person can't tell what's hidden meaning and what isn't, and the beliefs he takes in at that age tend to become fixed and hard to shift. That's why we should do everything to make sure the first stories they hear are composed as finely as possible to lead them toward virtue.'
'That makes sense,' he said. 'But if someone pressed us on this and asked which stories we mean and what they are, what could we tell him?'

'Adeimantus,' I said, 'you and I aren't poets right now; we're founding a city. And the founders of a city should know the patterns the poets must follow in telling their stories, and forbid them to depart from those; but the founders don't have to compose the stories themselves.'
'True,' he said. 'But these patterns for stories about the gods, what would they be?'
'Something like this,' I said. 'Whatever the poetry, epic, lyric, or tragic, the god must always be portrayed as he really is.'
'He must.'
'And isn't the god in fact good, and so to be described as good?'
'Of course.'
'And nothing good is harmful, is it?'
'I think not.'
'And what isn't harmful does no harm?'
'Not at all.'
'And what does no harm does no evil?'
'No.'
'And what does no evil couldn't be the cause of any evil?'
'How could it be?'
'Well then, is the good beneficial?'
'Yes.'
'So it's the cause of doing well?'
'Yes.'
'Then the good isn't the cause of everything. It's the cause of the things that go well, but not of the things that go badly.'
'Absolutely,' he said.

'So the god, since he's good, can't be the cause of everything, as most people say. He's the cause of only a few things that happen to us, and not of most, since the good things in human life are far fewer than the bad. The good things we can attribute to no one but the god, but for the bad we must look for some other cause, not the god.'
'That seems perfectly true to me,' he said.
'So we mustn't accept it from Homer, or any other poet, when he foolishly makes this mistake about the gods and says that two jars'
'"stand on the threshold of Zeus, full of fates, one of good ones, the other of bad,"'
'and that the man to whom Zeus gives a mixture of the two'
'"meets now with evil and now with good,"'
'while the man Zeus gives only from the second jar, the unmixed bad,'
'"is driven by ravening hunger over the bright earth."'

'Nor will we accept that Zeus is for us "the steward of good and evil alike." And if anyone says that the breaking of the oaths and truces, which was really Pandarus's doing, was brought about by Athena and Zeus, we won't praise him for it; nor that the strife and judgment among the goddesses came from Themis and Zeus. Nor again may our young men hear what Aeschylus says, that'
'"a god plants guilt in men when he wants to ruin a house utterly."'

'If a poet writes of the sufferings of Niobe, the subject of the play those lines come from, or of the house of Pelops, or of the Trojan war, or anything like it, either we won't let him say these things are the work of a god, or, if he does, he must find just the kind of account we're now demanding: he must say the god did what was just and good, and that the people were better off being punished. But we won't let the poet say that those who pay the penalty are made wretched, and that a god did it to them. We'll allow him to say that the wicked were wretched because they needed punishing, and that in paying the penalty by the god's hand they were benefited. But that the god, who is good, became the cause of evil to anyone, this we must fight against with all our strength. No one, young or old, is to say it or hear it, in verse or in prose, if our city is to be well governed. Such things are unholy to say, harmful to us, and out of tune with themselves.'
'I'm with you,' he said, 'and I'd happily vote for this as a law.'
'So this will be one of our laws and patterns about the gods, the one our speakers and poets must work within: the god is not the cause of everything, but only of the things that are good.'
'And that's good enough,' he said.

'Now, what about a second pattern? Do you think the god is a sorcerer, able to appear treacherously in one form at one time and another at another, sometimes by actually changing himself and passing into many shapes, sometimes by deceiving us and making us think we see him so? Or is he simple, one being, less likely than anything else to step outside his own form?'
'I can't answer offhand,' he said.
'Then answer this. If something steps outside its own form, mustn't the change come either from itself or from something else?'
'It must.'

'And aren't the things in the best condition the least altered and disturbed by anything outside them? A body, for instance, by food and drink and exertion, or a growing plant by sun and wind and the like, isn't it the healthiest and strongest that's least changed by these?'
'Of course.'
'And wouldn't an external blow least confuse and disturb the soul that's bravest and wisest?'
'Yes.'
'And the same goes, I'd say, for all manufactured things, furniture, houses, clothing: the well-made and well-conditioned ones are least altered by time and by anything else that happens to them.'
'That's so.'
'So everything that's in good condition, whether by nature or craft or both, admits the least change from outside itself.'
'It seems so.'
'But surely the god, and everything that belongs to the god, is in every way in the best condition.'
'Of course.'
'So on this score the god would be the least likely of all things to take many shapes.'
'The least likely indeed.'
'Then would he change and alter himself?'
'Clearly,' he said, 'if he's altered at all.'
'And would he change himself into something better and finer, or into something worse and uglier than himself?'
'It would have to be into something worse,' he said, 'if he changes at all, since we can't say the god is lacking in any beauty or goodness.'
'Quite right,' I said. 'And given that, do you think anyone, god or man, would willingly make himself worse in any way?'
'Impossible,' he said.
'Then it's impossible for a god to want to alter himself. Being, it seems, as beautiful and as good as can be, each of them stays forever, simply, in his own form.'
'That follows absolutely, I'd say.'
'Then let none of the poets tell us, my friend, that'
'"the gods, disguised as strangers from far-off lands, / take every sort of shape and roam our cities."'
'And let no one tell lies about Proteus and Thetis, or bring on, in tragedy or any other poetry, a Hera disguised as a priestess collecting alms'
'"for the life-giving children of Inachus, the river of Argos."'

'And spare us many other lies of that kind. Nor should mothers, taken in by these poets, frighten their children with twisted versions of them, telling how certain gods prowl about by night in the likeness of all sorts of strangers, both blaspheming against the gods and turning their children into cowards.'
'Heaven forbid,' he said.
'But might the gods, though they don't change in themselves, still make us imagine they appear in all sorts of forms, by deceiving us and working sorcery on us?'
'Perhaps,' he said.
'What?' I said. 'Would a god be willing to lie, in word or deed, by putting some illusion before us?'
'I don't know,' he said.
'Don't you know,' I said, 'that the genuine lie, if I may call it that, is hated by all gods and men?'
'What do you mean?'
'I mean that no one willingly wants to be lied to in the most important part of himself, about the most important things. There, above all, a man dreads having a lie take hold.'
'I still don't follow,' he said.

'That's because you think I'm saying something grand,' I said. 'I only mean that to be lied to in the soul about reality, to be left ignorant there and to hold the lie in possession, is the thing all men least want; they loathe a lie in that place above all.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they certainly do.'

'And as I was just saying, this ignorance in the soul of the man who has been deceived, the lie lodged in the soul itself, is what would most truly be called a real lie. The lie in mere words is only a kind of copy of a state already in the soul, an image that comes after it, not the pure thing itself. Isn't that so?'
'Quite so.'
'So the real lie is hated not only by the gods but by men.'
'I think so.'

'But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it useful enough not to deserve hatred? Isn't it useful against enemies, or when one of the people we call friends, in a fit of madness or folly, is about to do some harm, and the lie becomes a kind of remedy that turns him aside? And in those stories we were just discussing, the ones about long ago, because we don't know the truth about how things were, we make our falsehood as much like the truth as we can, and so make even that useful.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's just how it is.'
'Well, in which of these ways is a lie useful to a god? Would he make his falsehood resemble the truth because he doesn't know the distant past?'
'That would be absurd,' he said.
'So there's nothing of the lying poet in a god.'
'I think not.'
'Would he lie, then, out of fear of his enemies?'
'Far from it.'
'Because of the folly or madness of his friends?'
'But no fool or madman,' he said, 'is a friend of the gods.'
'So there's no reason a god would lie?'
'None.'
'Then the divine, the spiritual, is in every way free of falsehood.'
'Completely.'
'So the god is altogether simple and true, in deed and in word. He doesn't change himself, and he doesn't deceive others, in waking life or in dreams, by signs, words, or visions.'
'That's just how it strikes me too, now that you put it this way,' he said.

'Then you agree,' I said, 'that this is our second pattern for speaking and composing about the gods: that they aren't sorcerers who change their shape, and they don't mislead us with lies, in word or deed.'
'I agree.'
'So while we praise much in Homer, we won't praise the dream Zeus sends to Agamemnon. And we won't praise Aeschylus when he has Thetis say that Apollo, singing at her wedding,'

'"dwelt on the children she would bear, their freedom from sickness, their long lives, / and, calling my whole lot blessed by heaven, / he sang a song of triumph and gladdened my heart. / I trusted that Phoebus's mouth, brimming with prophecy, / could not speak false. And yet he, the very one who sang, / who sat at the feast, who said all this, is the one / who killed my son."'

'When a poet says such things about the gods, we'll be angry, refuse him a chorus, and not let the teachers use his work to educate the young, if our guardians are to grow up god-fearing and godlike, as far as that's possible for a human being.'
'I'm wholly with you on these patterns,' he said, 'and I'd make them my laws.'

So those, I said, are our principles about the gods: the sort of tales to be told, and the sort never to be told, to our pupils from childhood on, if we want them to honor the gods and their parents, and to value friendship with one another.
'Yes,' he said, 'and I think our principles are right.'
'But if they're to be brave, don't they need other lessons besides these, lessons of the kind that take away the fear of death? Can any man be brave with the fear of death inside him?'
'Certainly not,' he said.
'And can a man be fearless of death, can he choose death in battle over defeat and slavery, if he believes the world below is real and terrible?'
'Impossible.'

'So we'll have to keep a watch over the storytellers in this department too, just as in the others, and ask them to stop simply running down the world below and instead to speak well of it. Their gloomy descriptions aren't true, we'll tell them, and they'll do harm to men who are meant to be warriors.'
'Yes, that will be our task,' he said.
'Then we'll have to strike out a great many offending passages,' I said, 'starting with lines like these:'
'"I'd rather be a serf, bound to the soil of some poor, landless man, than rule as king over all the dead who are gone."'
'And we'll have to cut the verse that tells how Pluto dreaded',
'"lest those grim and moldering halls, which even the gods abhor, be laid open to the eyes of mortals and immortals alike."'
'And again:'
'"Good god — so even in the house of Hades there is something, a soul, a phantom shape, but no real mind in it at all!"'
'And the line about Tiresias:'
'"To him alone, even in death, Persephone granted understanding, that he alone should keep his wits; the rest are flitting shadows."'
'And again:'
'"The soul flew from his limbs and was gone to Hades, mourning its fate, leaving manhood and youth behind."'
'And again:'
'"And the soul, with a thin cry, slipped away like smoke beneath the earth."'
'And:'
'"As bats in the depths of some eerie cave, when one of them drops from the cluster on the rock, fly squeaking and cling to one another, so did the souls go squeaking on their way together."'

'We'll ask Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we cross out these passages and others like them. It isn't that they aren't fine poetry, or that the crowd doesn't enjoy them. It's the opposite: the more beautiful the poetry, the less fit it is for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free, and who ought to fear slavery more than death.'
'No doubt about it,' he said.

'And we'll also have to throw out all the dreadful, hair-raising names for the world below: Cocytus and Styx, ghosts beneath the earth, withered shades, all those words whose very mention sends a shudder through the soul of anyone who hears them. I'm not saying such horror stories don't serve some purpose. But there's a danger that they'll leave our guardians too jumpy, too soft.'
'Yes, that's a real danger,' he said.
'Then no more of them.'
'Right.'
'We need a different note struck instead, a nobler one to compose and sing.'
'Clearly.'
'And shall we also get rid of the wailing and lamenting of famous men?'
'They'll have to go with the rest.'
'But are we right to get rid of them? Think it through. Our principle is that a good man won't regard death as a terrible thing for another good man, his comrade.'
'Yes, that's our principle.'
'So he won't grieve for his friend's death as though something terrible had happened to him.'
'He won't.'
'We also hold that a man like this is sufficient unto himself for living well, and so, more than anyone, he doesn't depend on others.'
'True,' he said.
'So losing a son or a brother, or losing his money, is less terrible to him than to any other man.'
'Far less.'
'So he'll be the least likely to mourn, and he'll bear it with the greatest calm when some such loss falls on him.'
'Yes, he'll feel it much less than the rest.'

'So we'll be right to strip away the laments of famous men, and hand them over to women, and not even respectable women at that, and to second-rate men, so that those we're training to guard our country will be ashamed to behave like that.'
'Quite right.'

'Then once again we'll beg Homer and the other poets not to show us Achilles, the son of a goddess, tossing from his side to his back to his face, then leaping up and pacing in a frenzy along the shore of the barren sea, or scooping up the black ashes in both hands and pouring them over his head, weeping and wailing in all the ways Homer describes. And not to show Priam, a kinsman of the gods, begging and pleading,',
'"rolling in the dung, crying out to each man by name."'
'Still more earnestly we'll beg them at least not to bring the gods on stage in mourning, saying things like',
'"Misery, misery — that I bore the bravest of men to my sorrow."'
'And if they must bring the gods on at all, at least let them not dare to misrepresent the greatest of the gods so badly as to make him say:'
'"With my own eyes I see a man I love chased round and round the city walls, and my heart aches for him."'
'Or again:'
'"Alas, that Sarpedon, the man I love best of all, is fated to fall at the hands of Patroclus, the son of Menoetius."'

'Because, my dear Adeimantus, if our young men take such things seriously and don't laugh them off as unworthy, then none of them will think it beneath himself, a mere man, to behave the same way. He'll feel no shame, no restraint, at wailing and moaning over the smallest setback.'
'That's very true,' he said.
'It is. But, as our argument has just shown us, that's exactly what shouldn't happen, and we have to stand by that until someone gives us a better argument.'
'No, it shouldn't happen.'
'And our guardians shouldn't be too fond of laughter, either. As a rule, when a man gives way to violent laughter, a violent reaction follows.'
'I think that's so,' he said.
'So we won't allow worthy men, even ordinary mortals, to be shown overcome with laughter, and still less the gods.'
'Much less the gods,' he said.
'So we won't accept lines like Homer's, where he tells how',
'"unquenchable laughter broke out among the blessed gods, when they saw Hephaestus puffing and limping about the hall."'
'By your principles, we can't allow it.'
'Call them my principles if you like,' he said. 'Either way, we certainly can't allow it.'

'And then there's truth, which we must value highly. For if we were right earlier that a lie is useless to the gods and useful to men only as a kind of medicine, then plainly that medicine should be left to doctors. Private citizens have no business with it.'
'No business at all,' he said.

'So if anyone is to have the privilege of lying, it should be the rulers of the city, lying for the good of the city in dealings with enemies or even with their own citizens. No one else may touch it. For a private man to lie to the rulers is as grave a fault, worse, even, than for a patient to lie to his doctor about his own body, or an athlete to his trainer, or a sailor to fail to tell the captain the true state of the ship and the crew, how he and his shipmates are really doing.'
'Very true,' he said.
'So if the ruler catches anyone else in the city lying, any of the craftsmen,',
'"prophet, healer of the sick, or worker in wood,"'
'he'll punish him for introducing something as ruinous and destructive to the city as it would be to a ship.'
'He certainly will, if our city is ever actually built,' he said.
'Next, our young men have to be self-controlled.'
'Of course.'
'And aren't the main elements of self-control, broadly speaking, obeying those in command and ruling oneself in the pleasures of food, drink, and sex?'
'I think so.'
'Then we'll approve of words like Diomede's in Homer:'
'"Friend, sit still and do as I tell you,"'
'and the lines that follow,'
'"the Greeks marched on, breathing fury, in silent awe of their commanders,"'
'and other passages of that kind.'
'We will.'
'But what about a line like this:'
'"You drunk, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer,"'
'and the words after it? Are such things, and any other backtalk that private men in poetry or prose throw at their rulers, well said or badly said?'
'Badly.'
'They may be amusing enough, but they do nothing for self-control, and so they're likely to harm our young men. You'd agree with that?'
'Yes.'
'And then to make the wisest of men say that, to his mind, nothing is finer than',
'"when the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the steward draws wine from the bowl and carries it round and fills the cups"',
'is that a fit thing, or good for self-control, for a young man to hear? Or the verse',
'"the saddest of fates is to die and meet your doom from hunger"?'

'And what about the tale of Zeus? While the other gods and men slept and he alone lay awake, plotting his schemes, he forgot them all in an instant out of lust, and was so undone at the sight of Hera that he wouldn't even go inside, but wanted to take her right there on the ground, saying he'd never wanted her so much, not even the first time they came together',
'"in secret from their parents."'
'Or that other tale, of how Hephaestus chained up Ares and Aphrodite for the same sort of carrying-on?'
'No,' he said, 'I'm strongly of the opinion that they shouldn't hear that kind of thing.'
'But where famous men show real endurance, in word or deed, those passages they ought to see and hear. For instance the lines:'
'"He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: 'Endure, my heart; you have endured far worse than this.'"'
'Yes, certainly,' he said.
'And we mustn't let them be men who take bribes or love money.'
'Certainly not.'
'So we won't sing them lines like',
'"gifts win over gods, and gifts win over revered kings."'

'Nor will we praise Phoenix, Achilles's tutor, or call him a wise counselor for telling Achilles to take the Greeks' gifts and help them, but to hold on to his anger if no gift came. Nor will we believe, or admit, that Achilles himself was such a lover of money that he accepted Agamemnon's gifts, or that he gave back Hector's corpse only for a ransom and wouldn't have done it otherwise.'
'No,' he said, 'those aren't sentiments anyone could approve.'

'Much as I love Homer,' I said, 'I'm reluctant even to say it, but to fasten these feelings on Achilles, or to believe others who do, comes close to outright impiety. The same with the story of his insolence to Apollo, when he says,',
'"You have cheated me, far-shooter, cruelest of the gods. I would pay you back, if only I had the power."'

'And his defiance of the river-god, on whom he was ready to lay hands; and his cutting off his own hair for the dead Patroclus, hair already vowed to another river, Spercheius, and actually going through with it; and his dragging Hector around Patroclus's tomb, and butchering captives on the pyre. None of this can I believe he really did. Nor can I let our citizens believe that Achilles, the pupil of the wise Cheiron, son of a goddess and of Peleus, the gentlest of men and third in line from Zeus, was so disordered in his mind as to be torn at once between two contradictory diseases, a mean streak shot through with greed, and at the same time an arrogant contempt for gods and men alike.'
'You're quite right,' he said.

'And let's equally refuse to believe, or to let anyone repeat, the tale of Theseus, son of Poseidon, and Pirithous, son of Zeus, setting out to commit terrible abductions, or of any other hero or son of a god daring to do the dreadful, unholy things they now slanderously pin on them. Let's force the poets either to deny that these were the gods' deeds, or to deny that the men were the sons of gods. They can't have it both ways. And we won't let them try to convince our young men that the gods are the source of evil and that the heroes were no better than ordinary men. As we said before, that's neither holy nor true, since we already proved that evil can't come from the gods.'
'No, it can't.'
'And besides, such stories do real damage to those who hear them, because every man will start excusing his own vices once he's convinced that this is just how things are done by',
'"the gods' own kindred, the close relatives of Zeus, whose ancestral altar of Zeus stands high in the air on the peak of Ida,"',
'and in whom',
'"the blood of the gods still runs."'
'So let's put a stop to such tales, before they breed a slack and lawless spirit in the young.'
'By all means,' he said.

'Now, since we're deciding which kinds of subject may and may not be spoken of, let's check whether we've left anything out. How gods, demigods, heroes, and the world below are to be handled, we've already settled.'
'We have.'
'And what should we say about men? That's plainly the part left over.'
'Plainly.'
'But we can't answer that yet, my friend.'
'Why not?'

'Because, unless I'm mistaken, we'd have to say that poets and storytellers go badly wrong about men, in claiming that plenty of unjust men are happy and just men miserable; that injustice pays, as long as you aren't caught; and that justice is another man's good and your own loss. We'll forbid them to say such things and order them to sing and tell the opposite.'
'We certainly will,' he said.
'But if you grant I'm right about that, then I'll say you've conceded the very thing we've been arguing for all along.'
'I accept that this follows,' he said.

'Whether such things are to be said about men is a question we can't settle until we've discovered what justice is, and how, by its very nature, it benefits whoever has it, whether or not he seems just to others.'
'Very true,' he said.
'So much for the content of poetry. Now let's talk about its style or manner, and once we've done that, we'll have covered both what to say and how to say it.'
'I don't follow you,' said Adeimantus.
'Then I'll have to make you follow,' I said. 'Maybe I can put it this way. You know, I take it, that all storytelling and poetry is a narrative of things past, present, or to come?'
'Of course,' he said.
'And the narrating is done either by plain narration, or by impersonation, or by a mix of the two?'
'There again,' he said, 'I don't quite follow.'

'I must be a laughable teacher,' I said, 'if I'm having this much trouble making myself clear. Like a poor speaker, then, I won't take the whole subject at once. I'll break off a piece of it to show you what I mean. You know the opening of the Iliad, where the poet tells how Chryses begged Agamemnon to release his daughter, and how Agamemnon flew into a rage, so that Chryses, failing in his plea, called down the god's anger on the Achaeans. Now up to the lines',
'"and he begged all the Greeks, but the two sons of Atreus above all, the marshals of the host,"'

'the poet speaks in his own voice. He never tries to make us think he's someone else. But after that he speaks as if he were Chryses himself, doing everything he can to make us believe the speaker isn't Homer but the old priest. And he's cast nearly the whole of the Iliad and the Odyssey in this double form.'
'Yes.'
'And it's all narrative, both in the speeches he gives us and in the passages between them?'
'Of course.'
'But when he delivers a speech in someone else's character, don't we say he makes his style as much like that person's as he can?'
'We do.'
'And making yourself like someone else, in voice or gesture, is impersonating the one whose character you've taken on?'
'Certainly.'
'So in these passages the poet's narrative works by impersonation?'
'Just so.'

'But where the poet never hides himself, the impersonation drops away and his poetry becomes plain narration. So that you can't say once more, "I don't follow," let me show how this would work. If Homer, after saying the priest came with his daughter's ransom to plead with the Achaeans and above all the kings, had gone on speaking in his own voice instead of as Chryses, the result wouldn't be impersonation but plain narration. It would run something like this, in prose, since I'm no poet: "The priest came and prayed that the gods would grant the Greeks the capture of Troy and a safe return home, but begged them, out of reverence for the god, to release his daughter and accept the ransom. The other Greeks heard him with respect and approved. But Agamemnon was furious and ordered him to leave and not come back, or his staff and the god's garlands would do him no good. The girl, he said, would not be freed; she'd grow old in Argos at his side. He told the priest to go away and not provoke him, if he wanted to get home safe. The old man was afraid and went off in silence, and once clear of the camp he prayed long to Apollo, calling on all his titles and reminding the god of every temple he'd built and every sacrifice he'd made, and asked that in return his tears be paid back by the god's arrows on the Achaeans." That's how the whole thing becomes plain narrative.'
'I understand,' he said.
'Now picture the opposite case: the connecting passages cut out, and only the dialogue left.'
'That I understand too,' he said. 'You mean the way it's done in tragedy.'

'You've got my meaning exactly,' I said. 'And now I think what you couldn't grasp before is clear: poetry and storytelling come in three kinds. One is wholly impersonation, as in tragedy and comedy. Another is the poet speaking throughout in his own voice, best seen in the dithyramb. And the third combines the two, as in epic and in several other forms. Are you with me?'
'Yes,' he said, 'now I see what you meant.'
'Then remember what I said when we started, that we were finished with the content and ready to move to the manner.'
'I remember.'

'What I was getting at is that we have to come to an agreement about impersonation. Should we allow the poets to tell their stories by impersonation? And if so, should it be all impersonation, or only part, and if part, which parts? Or should impersonation be banned altogether?'
'I suspect,' he said, 'you're asking whether we'll admit tragedy and comedy into our city.'
'Perhaps,' I said. 'But there may be more to it than that. I don't quite know yet. Wherever the argument blows us, like a wind, there we'll go.'
'And go we will,' he said.

'Then tell me this, Adeimantus. Should our guardians be impersonators or not? Hasn't this already been settled by the rule we laid down, that one man can do one thing well, not many, and that if he tries his hand at many he'll fail to make his mark at any?'
'It has.'
'And the same goes for impersonation: no one man can imitate many things as well as he can imitate one.'
'No, he can't.'

'So a man will hardly be able to live a serious life and at the same time impersonate a whole range of characters. Even two closely related kinds of imitation, like writing tragedy and writing comedy, are beyond the same person, aren't they? You did just now call these imitations?'
'I did, and you're right that the same men can't do both.'
'No more than they can be both reciters and actors at once?'
'True.'
'And the same actors don't play in both comedy and tragedy, though all of these are imitations?'
'They don't.'

'Human nature, Adeimantus, seems to me to be minted into still smaller coins than that, so that no one can imitate many things well, any more than he can actually do well the many things the imitations are copies of.'
'Very true,' he said.

'So if we hold to our original idea, that our guardians must set everything else aside and devote themselves wholly to keeping the city free, making this their one craft and taking up no work that doesn't serve that end, then they shouldn't do or imitate anything else. Or if they do imitate, let them imitate from childhood only what's suited to their calling: the brave, the self-controlled, the holy, the free, and so on. But meanness they shouldn't imitate, or anything else shameful, in case the imitation breeds the reality. Have you noticed how imitations, kept up from youth far into life, settle into habits and become a man's second nature, in body, voice, and mind?'
'I certainly have,' he said.

'Then we won't let those we care about, the men we say must be good, imitate a woman, young or old, railing at her husband, or quarreling with the gods and boasting because she thinks herself so happy, or sunk in grief and mourning; and we'll certainly forbid them to imitate a woman in sickness, in love, or in childbirth.'
'Quite right,' he said.
'Nor may they imitate slaves, male or female, doing slaves' work.'
'No.'

'Nor, surely, bad men, cowards and the rest, who do the opposite of all we've prescribed, jeering and mocking and abusing each other, drunk or sober, sinning against themselves and others in word and deed, as such men do. And they shouldn't be trained to imitate the words or actions of the mad, either. They have to recognize madness and badness, but not act them out or imitate them.'
'Very true,' he said.
'And may they imitate smiths or other craftsmen at their work, or rowers, or the men who keep time for them, or anything of that sort?'
'How could they,' he said, 'when they aren't even allowed to turn their minds to any of those trades?'
'And may they imitate horses neighing, bulls bellowing, the rush of rivers, the roar of the sea, thunder, and all the rest of it?'
'No,' he said, 'if they're forbidden to be mad, they can't go acting like madmen either.'
'If I follow you,' I said, 'there's one kind of narrative style a truly good man will use when he has something to say, and another that a man of the opposite character and upbringing will use.'
'And what are these two?' he asked.

'Suppose,' I said, 'that a good and decent man, in the course of a story, comes to some speech or action of another good man. I imagine he'll be glad to deliver it as if he were that man, and won't be ashamed of imitating him, least of all when the good man is acting steadily and sensibly, less so when illness or love or drink or some other misfortune has overtaken him. But when he comes to someone unworthy of him, he won't be willing to model himself on a worse man in earnest. He'll do it, if at all, only for a moment, when the worse man happens to do something good, and even then he'll be ashamed, since he's never practiced shaping himself to baser models, and his whole nature rebels against it, unless it's all in fun.'
'That's what I'd expect,' he said.
'So he'll use the kind of narrative we found in Homer, both impersonation and plain narration, but with very little of the first and a great deal of the second. Do you agree?'
'Certainly,' he said. 'That has to be the model for such a speaker.'

'But there's the other sort of man, who'll narrate anything, and the worse he is the less he'll hold back. Nothing is beneath him. He'll set out to imitate everything, and in dead earnest, before a big crowd. As I said, he'll try to give us the crash of thunder, the howl of wind and hail, the creak of axles and pulleys, the blare of flutes and pipes and trumpets and every other instrument. He'll bark like a dog, bleat like a sheep, crow like a rooster. His whole art will be imitation, of sound and gesture, with hardly any narration at all.'
'That'll be his way of telling a story,' he said.
'So these are the two kinds of style?'
'Yes.'

'And you'll agree that one of them allows only slight changes, so that if you also pick a harmony and a rhythm to match its simplicity, a man who speaks it correctly stays nearly the same throughout, keeping to a single harmony, since the changes are small, and to roughly one rhythm?'
'Quite true,' he said.
'Whereas the other kind needs every harmony and every rhythm, if the music is to fit the words, because it's full of changes of every sort.'
'That's perfectly true too,' he said.
'And don't all poets, and everyone who speaks at all, use one or the other of these styles, or a mix of both?'
'They cover everything,' he said.
'So shall we admit all of them into our city, or just one of the two unmixed kinds, or the mixed one?'
'If it were up to me,' he said, 'I'd admit only the pure imitator of the good man.'
'And yet, Adeimantus, the mixed style is very charming, and the one most opposite to your choice, the all-imitating style, is what children and their attendants and the mass of people love best.'
'I don't deny it,' he said.
'But I suppose you'd say it doesn't suit our city, where no man is two men or many, but each plays one part only?'
'Yes, it doesn't suit us.'

'And that's why ours is the only city where you'll find a shoemaker who's a shoemaker and not also a ship's pilot, a farmer who's a farmer and not also a juror, a soldier who's a soldier and not also a trader, and so on right through.'
'True,' he said.

'So if one of these clever, do-anything men, who can imitate the whole world, came to our city and offered to put himself and his poems on show, we'd bow down to him as a holy and marvelous and delightful creature, but we'd tell him there's no place for a man like him in our city, the law won't allow it, and then we'd anoint his head with myrrh, crown him with wool, and send him off to some other city. For our own souls' sake we'll keep the plainer, sterner poet and storyteller, the one who imitates only the style of the good man, and who keeps to the standards we laid down at the start when we began educating our soldiers.'
'That's certainly what we'll do,' he said, 'if it's in our power.'
