'Then, my friend,' I said, 'that part of education in music and poetry that has to do with story and myth seems to be finished. We've covered both the content and the manner.'
'I think so too,' he said.
'Next in line comes the matter of melody and song.'
'Obviously.'
'And by now anyone can see what we should say about them, if we mean to be consistent.'
Glaucon laughed. 'I'm afraid I may not count as "anyone,"' he said, 'because at this moment I can't quite say what we should hold, though I have a guess.'
'Well, at any rate,' I said, 'you can certainly say this much: a song has three parts, the words, the harmony, and the rhythm.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that much I can.'
'And as for the words, there'll be no difference between words set to music and words not set to music. Both have to obey the same rules we've already laid down.'
'Yes.'
'And the harmony and rhythm have to follow the words.'
'Of course.'
'And we said we had no need of dirges and laments. So which are the harmonies that express grief? You're musical; tell me.'
'The mixed Lydian,' he said, 'and the high-pitched Lydian, and others of that sort.'
'Then those must be banished,' I said. 'They're useless even to women who are to be of any worth, let alone to men.'
'Certainly.'
'And drunkenness, softness, and idleness are wholly unbecoming in our guardians.'
'Wholly.'
'Which are the soft, drinking-party harmonies?'
'The Ionian,' he said, 'and certain Lydian modes that are called "slack."'
'And are these any use to fighting men?'
'Quite the opposite,' he said. 'So you're left with the Dorian and the Phrygian.'

'I know nothing about the harmonies myself,' I said. 'But leave me one that will fittingly imitate the voice and the bearing of a brave man in the thick of battle and in every grim necessity, when his cause is going badly and he faces wounds or death or some other disaster, and in all of it stands firm and endures. And leave me another for a man at peace, acting freely, under no compulsion: persuading a god by prayer or a man by teaching and advice, or, on the other side, opening himself to another's appeal or instruction or warning, and so, by good sense, getting his way, not carried off by success but acting soberly and moderately throughout, content with how things turn out. Those two harmonies, the strain of necessity and the strain of freedom, of the unfortunate man and the fortunate, of courage and of self-control, those I ask you to leave us.'
'But those,' he said, 'are exactly the two I was just speaking of, the Dorian and the Phrygian.'
'Then if these and only these are to be used in our songs and melodies,' I said, 'we won't need a great range of notes or an instrument that runs through every scale.'
'It seems not.'
'So we won't keep the makers of three-cornered harps and many-stringed instruments, or anyone who builds instruments tuned to every mode.'
'Apparently not.'

'And what about flute-makers and flute-players? Will you admit them, when you consider that the flute is the most many-noted instrument of all, and that the instruments tuned to every mode are really only imitations of it?'
'Clearly not,' he said.
'So you're left with the lyre and the kithara for use in the city, and out in the country the herdsmen can have some sort of pipe.'
'That's certainly what the argument suggests,' he said.
'And we're doing nothing strange,' I said, 'in preferring Apollo and Apollo's instruments to Marsyas and his.'
'Nothing strange at all,' he said.
'By the dog of Egypt,' I said, 'without noticing it we've been purging the city we called luxurious a little while ago.'
'And very sensibly too,' he said.

'Then let's finish the purge. After harmonies comes rhythm, which should follow the same rules. We shouldn't go chasing complicated systems of meter, or every kind of measure, but should find out which rhythms express a brave and orderly life, and then fit the meter and the tune to words of that spirit, not the words to the meter and the tune. As for what those rhythms are, that's for you to tell me, the way you told me about the harmonies.'

'I really can't,' he said. 'I do know there are roughly three basic kinds of rhythm out of which the meters are built, just as there are four notes in sound out of which all the harmonies come, and I've observed that much. But which of them imitate which sort of life, I can't say.'

'Then we'll have to bring Damon into the discussion,' I said, 'and let him tell us which rhythms suit meanness, or arrogance, or madness, or other base things, and which should be kept for their opposites. I have a vague memory of him mentioning a complex marching rhythm, and a dactylic or heroic one, which he arranged somehow I don't quite grasp, balancing the rise and fall of the foot equally, long against short. And I think he spoke of an iambic and a trochaic, assigning short and long quantities to them. In some cases I believe he praised or blamed the tempo of the foot as much as the rhythm itself, or perhaps a combination of the two, I'm not sure. But as I say, let's leave all this to Damon, since untangling it would take a long argument. Don't you agree?'
'I certainly do,' he said.
'But this much you can see without any trouble: gracefulness, or its absence, goes with good or bad rhythm.'
'Of course.'

'And good rhythm naturally goes with a fine style, and bad rhythm with its opposite, and the same with harmony and discord, since rhythm and harmony, as we said, follow the words, not the other way around.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they should follow the words.'
'And don't the words and the style depend on the character of the soul?'
'Naturally.'
'And everything else follows the style?'
'Yes.'

'So fine speech, fine harmony, gracefulness, and good rhythm all follow from a good character, by which I don't mean the silliness we politely call good nature, but a mind and character truly well and nobly ordered.'
'Quite so,' he said.
'And mustn't our young men aim at these everywhere, if they're going to do their proper work?'
'They must.'

'And surely painting is full of these same qualities, and so is every other craft of making, weaving, embroidery, building, the making of any object at all, and nature too, in living bodies and growing things. In all of them there's gracefulness or its lack. And ugliness, bad rhythm, and discord are close kin to bad speech and bad character, while their opposites are kin to, and copies of, the opposite: a sober and good character.'
'Absolutely,' he said.

'So is it only the poets we have to oversee, forcing them to put the image of good character into their poems or else not work among us? Or should we keep watch over the other craftsmen too, and stop them from setting the stamp of bad character, of intemperance, meanness, and indecency, on their paintings and buildings and other works? Anyone who can't do this shouldn't be allowed to practice his craft in our city, so that our guardians won't be raised among images of vice, as if in some poisoned pasture, where day after day they'd graze and feed on much that is harmful, a little at a time, until without noticing they piled up one great festering corruption in their souls. We should look instead for the craftsmen with the gift to track down the nature of the beautiful and graceful, so that our young men, living as in a healthy place, will take good from every quarter, wherever some fine work strikes their eyes or ears, like a breeze off clean ground bringing health, and from earliest childhood will be drawn, without their knowing it, into likeness and friendship and harmony with the beauty of reason.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that would be far the finest upbringing.'

'And isn't this why education in music and poetry is so powerful, Glaucon? Because rhythm and harmony sink deepest into the soul and take the firmest hold of it, bringing gracefulness in their train, so that they make a man graceful if he's rightly brought up, and graceless if he isn't. And the man rightly educated in this way will have the sharpest eye for what's left out or badly made in any work of craft or of nature. His distaste will be just; he'll praise and welcome into his soul the beautiful things and be nourished by them and grow noble and good, while still a child, before he can give the reason, he'll rightly condemn and hate the ugly ones, and when reason comes at last, he'll greet it as a friend, because his upbringing has made him familiar with it all along.'
'Yes,' he said, 'I think that's just why education in music and poetry matters so much.'

'It's like learning to read,' I said. 'We weren't satisfied until we could pick out the letters, few as they are, in all their combinations, never treating them as beneath notice whether they appeared in something large or small, but everywhere eager to make them out, knowing we wouldn't be readers until we could.'
'True.'
'And we can't recognize the reflections of letters in water or in a mirror until we know the letters themselves, since both belong to the same skill and the same study.'
'Exactly.'

'Then, by the same token, neither we nor the guardians we're educating can become musical until we can recognize the basic forms of self-control, courage, generosity, greatness of soul, and their kindred, and their opposites too, wherever they turn up, in things great or small, knowing that all of it belongs to one and the same skill and study.'
'That must be so,' he said.
'And when a beautiful character in the soul agrees with a beautiful form in the body, both cast in one mold, won't that be the fairest sight of all to anyone with eyes to see it?'
'The fairest of all.'
'And the fairest is also the most lovable?'
'Naturally.'
'So the truly musical man will love such people most, but won't love anyone whose soul is out of tune.'
'No,' he said, 'not if the flaw is in the soul. If it's only some bodily defect, he'll be patient and willing to love the person all the same.'
'I see,' I said, 'that you have, or have had, a beloved of that kind, and I won't argue. But tell me this: does extravagant pleasure have anything in common with self-control?'
'How could it,' he said, 'when pleasure throws the mind off balance as much as pain does?'
'And anything in common with virtue generally?'
'Nothing at all.'
'But with violence and lack of control?'
'More than anything.'
'And can you name a greater or keener pleasure than sex?'
'No,' he said, 'nor a more frenzied one.'
'But the right kind of love is a love of what's beautiful and orderly, a self-controlled and harmonious love.'
'Quite true,' he said.
'So nothing frenzied, nothing akin to a lack of self-control, should come anywhere near the right kind of love.'
'No, it shouldn't.'
'So this mad, intemperate pleasure must never come near the lover and the one he loves; neither of them can have any share in it, if their love is the right kind.'
'No, Socrates,' he said, 'it must never come near them.'

'So it seems you'll lay down a law, in the city we're founding, that a lover may show his beloved no greater intimacy than a father would show a son, and that only for a fine end, and only with the other's consent. This is to govern all his dealings with the boy he cares for, and he must never be seen going further. If he does, he'll be branded as coarse and without taste.'
'I quite agree,' he said.
'And there, I think, our talk of music and poetry comes to its proper end, since it has ended where talk of these things should end, in the love of the beautiful.'
'I agree,' he said.
'After music and poetry, our young men must be trained in physical exercise.'
'Of course.'

'And here too the training should start in childhood and go on carefully through life. My own view, and I'd like to hear yours to confirm it, is that it isn't a good body that makes the soul good by its own excellence, but the other way around: a good soul, by its own excellence, makes the body as good as it can be. What do you say?'
'I agree,' he said.
'So if we give the mind a thorough training and then hand over to it the detailed care of the body, we'll be doing the right thing. To keep this short, let me just sketch the outline.'
'Go ahead.'
'We already said the guardians must keep off drink. Of all men a guardian is the last who should get drunk and not know where on earth he is.'
'Yes,' he said, 'it would be absurd for a guardian to need another guardian to look after him.'
'And what about their food? These men are athletes in the greatest of all contests, aren't they?'
'They are.'
'Would the regime of our ordinary athletes suit them?'
'Perhaps.'

'I'm afraid that's a drowsy sort of training,' I said, 'and risky for the health. Haven't you noticed how these athletes sleep their lives away, and how they fall dangerously ill the moment they stray even slightly from their fixed routine?'
'I have.'

'Then our warrior-athletes need a finer kind of training. They have to be like wakeful watchdogs, with the keenest sight and hearing, and on campaign they'll have to put up with every change of water and food, with summer heat and winter cold, without their health giving way.'
'That's my view too.'
'And the best physical training is the twin sister of the simple music we were just describing.'
'How so?'
'I mean there's a kind of physical training that's simple and good, just as our music was, and especially the training for war.'
'What do you mean?'

'You can learn it from Homer. You know how he feeds his heroes on campaign: no fish, even though they're camped on the shores of the Hellespont, and no boiled meat, only roast, which is what suits soldiers best, since all they need is a fire, and they don't have to lug pots around.'
'True.'
'And I think I'm right that Homer nowhere mentions rich sauces. In fact every athlete in training knows that a man who wants to stay in condition must keep off that sort of thing.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they know it, and they're right to keep off it.'
'Then you wouldn't approve of Syracusan dinners and the elaborate dishes of Sicilian cooking?'
'I think not.'
'Nor would you let a man who means to stay in condition keep a Corinthian girl as his sweetheart?'
'Certainly not.'
'Nor would you approve of those famous Athenian pastries?'
'No.'
'All such food and such living we can fairly compare to a song and a melody composed in every mode and every rhythm at once.'
'Exactly.'
'There the complexity bred license, and here it breeds disease; whereas simplicity in music bred self-control in the soul, and simplicity in physical training breeds health in the body.'
'Very true,' he said.

'And when license and disease multiply in a city, don't they keep throwing open more courtrooms and clinics, so that law and medicine start giving themselves airs, when even free men, not just slaves, take them so seriously?'
'Of course.'

'And what greater sign could there be of a bad, disgraceful education than this: that not only the laborers and common people need first-rate doctors and judges, but men who claim to have had a liberal upbringing need them too? Isn't it shameful, a glaring mark of bad breeding, that a man should have to go to others for his justice, as if to lords and masters, having none of his own inside him?'
'The most shameful thing of all,' he said.

'Would you call it "the most" shameful,' I said, 'when there's a worse stage still? When a man not only spends his whole life in the courts, suing and being sued, but is so devoid of taste that he actually prides himself on his skill at wrongdoing, sure that he's a master at it, able to twist every which way, slip through any loophole, bend like a reed to dodge a verdict, all to win paltry points not worth mentioning, not knowing how much finer and nobler it is to order one's life so as never to need a drowsy judge at all?'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's still more shameful.'

'And to need medicine,' I said, 'not for a wound or one of the seasonal illnesses, but just because, through idleness and the kind of living we've described, a man fills himself up with fluids and gases like a stagnant marsh, and forces the clever sons of Asclepius to invent names for diseases, "flatulence" and "catarrh" and the rest, isn't that a disgrace too?'
'It is,' he said. 'Those really are strange new-fangled names for diseases.'

'The kind, I think, that didn't exist in Asclepius's day,' I said. 'I infer this from the fact that at Troy, when Eurypylus was wounded, no one objected to the girl who gave him Pramnian wine sprinkled with barley meal and grated cheese to drink, things you'd think highly inflammatory, and the sons of Asclepius there didn't blame Patroclus, who was treating him.'
'It was certainly an odd drink,' he said, 'for a man in that state.'

'Not so odd,' I said, 'if you remember that before Herodicus's time the school of Asclepius didn't practice our present kind of medicine, the kind that nurses diseases along. Herodicus was a trainer who fell sick, and by mixing training with doctoring he found a way to torment first himself and then the rest of the world.'
'How so?' he asked.

'By inventing the lingering death. He had a fatal illness, and by tending it endlessly, since there was no cure, he dragged out his whole life as an invalid. He could do nothing but nurse himself, in agony whenever he strayed from his routine, and so, by his cleverness, he died hard, and slowly, all the way into old age.'
'A fine reward for his skill,' he said.

'Just what you'd expect,' I said, 'for a man who never understood that Asclepius left his descendants no instruction in this invalid's art, not out of ignorance, but because he knew that in a well-run city every man has his own work to do and no leisure to spend a lifetime being ill. We see this clearly in the case of the craftsman, but, absurdly, we don't apply it to the rich.'
'How do you mean?' he said.

'I mean this. When a carpenter falls ill, he asks his doctor for a quick remedy: something to make him vomit, or move his bowels, or a cautery, or the knife. If the doctor prescribes a long course of diet, wrapping his head up and all the rest, he says at once that he has no time to be ill, and sees no point in a life spent nursing his disease while his proper work goes neglected. So he says goodbye to that kind of doctor, goes back to his ordinary life, and either gets well and lives and does his work, or, if his body can't take it, dies and is out of his troubles.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the right way for a man in his station to use medicine.'
'Because he has work to do,' I said, 'and there's no profit in living if he can't do it.'
'Quite true,' he said.
'But the rich man is different. We don't say he has any appointed task he must do or else not live.'
'No, he's generally supposed to have nothing to do.'
'Then you've never heard the saying of Phocylides, that a man should practice virtue once he has a living?'
'I'd say he should start sooner than that,' he said.

'Let's not quarrel with Phocylides about that,' I said. 'Let's just ask ourselves: is the rich man, too, obliged to practice virtue, and is his life worthless without it? And if he is obliged, does this fussing over the body get in the way of practicing virtue, just as it gets in the way of carpentry and the other trades?'
'It certainly does,' he said. 'Excessive care of the body, beyond plain exercise, is about as great a hindrance to virtue as anything could be.'

'Yes,' I said, 'and it's just as incompatible with managing a household, serving in the army, or holding office in the city. Worst of all, it makes any kind of study or thought or quiet self-examination impossible, since the man is forever suspecting that his headaches and dizziness come from too much philosophy, so that wherever virtue in this higher sense is being practiced or tested, he's a hindrance, always imagining himself ill, always anxious about his body.'
'Very likely,' he said.

'So we'll say that Asclepius knew all this, and showed his art only to people who were generally sound in body and habits but had some specific complaint. These he cured with drugs or surgery and then told to go on living as usual, so as not to harm the city. But bodies riddled with disease all the way through he wouldn't try to patch up with slow drainings and infusions, drawing out a useless life and letting weak fathers breed still weaker sons. He thought a man who couldn't live the normal span of life shouldn't be treated, since such a cure would do no good to the man himself or to the city.'
'So you make Asclepius a statesman,' he said.

'Plainly he was one,' I said, 'and you can see it in his sons too. Notice that at Troy they fought bravely and practiced medicine the way I've described. You remember how, when Pandarus wounded Menelaus, they',
'"sucked out the blood and sprinkled soothing drugs on the wound,"'

'but never told him afterward what to eat or drink, any more than they did with Eurypylus. The remedies were enough to heal any man who'd been sound and orderly in his habits before the wound, even if he did happen to drink Pramnian wine. But men whose bodies were sickly and intemperate, whose lives were no use to themselves or anyone else, they thought medicine wasn't meant for, and they wouldn't treat them, not even if they were richer than Midas.'
'Very shrewd men, those sons of Asclepius,' he said.

'As you'd expect,' I said. 'And yet the tragic poets and Pindar, ignoring us, while they admit that Asclepius was Apollo's son, also say he was bribed into healing a rich man already at the point of death, and was struck by lightning for it. But by our principle we won't believe both claims. If he was a god's son, we'll say he wasn't greedy for money; and if he was greedy for money, he wasn't a god's son.'

'That part is excellent, Socrates,' he said. 'But here's a question for you. Shouldn't a city have good doctors? And aren't the best doctors the ones who've handled the greatest number of cases, healthy and sick alike? And aren't the best judges, likewise, those who've dealt with every kind of character?'
'Yes,' I said, 'I do want good doctors and good judges. But do you know which ones I think are good?'
'Tell me.'
'I will, if I can. But notice that you've lumped together two things that aren't alike.'
'How so?' he asked.

'You've put doctors and judges side by side. Now the most skillful doctors are the ones who, from youth up, have added to their knowledge of the art the widest experience of disease, and who'd do better not to have been robust in health themselves but to have suffered every illness in their own bodies. For they don't cure the body with the body; if they did, we couldn't let them be, or ever have been, sickly. They cure the body with the mind, and a mind that's become and stayed sick can cure nothing.'
'Very true,' he said.

'But with the judge it's the other way around, since he governs mind with mind. He shouldn't have been brought up among vicious minds and kept company with them from youth, running through the whole catalog of crime himself, just so that he can quickly infer other people's wrongs from his own, the way a doctor might infer a disease. No, the honest mind that's to judge soundly should have had no taste of bad habits, no infection from them, when young. That's why good men, when young, often seem naive and are easily taken in by the dishonest, because they have no pattern of wickedness in themselves to match against it.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that happens to them all the time.'

'So the good judge mustn't be young,' I said. 'He should be old, having learned late and slowly what evil is, not from his own soul but from watching it for a long time in others. Knowledge should be his guide, not personal experience.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the noblest kind of judge.'

'And a good man, too,' I said, 'which is the answer to your question, since a man is good who has a good soul. But that clever and suspicious type, the man who's done a great deal of wrong and thinks himself a master of cunning, is impressive at taking precautions among men like himself, because he measures them by his own standard. But when he comes among good and older men, he looks a fool again, with his unseasonable suspicions, because he can't recognize an honest man, having no pattern of honesty in himself. And since the bad outnumber the good and he meets them more often, he thinks himself wise, and others think so too, rather than foolish.'
'Very true,' he said.

'So this isn't the wise and good judge we're after, but the other,' I said. 'For badness can never know both virtue and itself, while a virtuous nature, educated over time, will come to know both virtue and vice. So it's the virtuous man, not the vicious one, who has wisdom, in my view.'
'And in mine too,' he said.

'Then this is the kind of medicine and the kind of law you'll establish in your city. They'll care for the citizens whose natures are sound in body and soul, but those whose bodies are unsound they'll let die, and those whose souls are rotten and incurable they'll put to death themselves.'
'That's clearly best,' he said, 'both for the men themselves and for the city.'
'And plainly your young men,' I said, 'brought up on that simple music that breeds self-control, will be slow to need the courts.'
'Clearly.'
'And the man trained in music, following the same path with simple physical training, will want nothing to do with medicine except in dire need.'
'I believe that,' he said.

'In fact he'll undergo his exercises and labors to rouse the spirited part of his nature rather than to build up strength. He won't, like ordinary athletes, use food and exercise just to put on muscle.'
'Quite right,' he said.
'And the two arts, music and physical training, aren't really meant, as people suppose, one for the soul and the other for the body.'
'Then what are they for?' he asked.
'I believe,' I said, 'that whoever teaches them aims chiefly at the soul.'
'How can that be?' he asked.
'Have you never noticed,' I said, 'what an exclusive devotion to physical training does to a man's character, and what the opposite, an exclusive devotion to music, does?'
'In what way?' he said.
'The one breeds hardness and savagery, the other softness and weakness.'
'Yes,' he said, 'I'm well aware that men who train only their bodies turn out too fierce, and those who give themselves only to music turn out softer than is good for them.'
'And yet,' I said, 'this fierceness comes from the spirited part of a man's nature, which, rightly trained, would be courage, but stretched too tight turns hard and brutal.'
'I quite think so,' he said.
'And gentleness belongs to the philosophic nature. Indulged too far it becomes softness, but rightly trained it's gentle and orderly.'
'True.'
'And our guardians, we say, need both these natures?'
'They do.'
'And the two must be in harmony with each other?'
'Of course.'
'And the man whose soul is in harmony is both self-controlled and brave.'
'Yes.'
'And the man whose soul is out of harmony is cowardly and coarse.'
'Very true.'

'So when a man lets music play over him and pours into his soul through his ears all those sweet, soft, mournful tunes we spoke of, and spends his whole life humming and lost in song, then at first, if he had any spirit, it's tempered like iron and made useful, instead of brittle and good for nothing. But if he keeps on, never letting up, the music begins to melt him down, until it dissolves his spirit and cuts the very sinews out of his soul, and he becomes a feeble warrior.'
'Very true,' he said.

'If his nature was short on spirit to begin with, this happens quickly. But if he had plenty of spirit, the music weakens it and leaves him touchy, flaring up over nothing and as quickly going out, peevish and irritable instead of spirited, and impossible to deal with.'
'Exactly.'

'Now suppose instead a man works himself hard at exercise and eats well, but never touches music or philosophy. At first, with his body in fine condition, he's full of confidence and spirit and becomes twice the man he was.'
'Certainly.'

'But what happens next? If he does nothing else and never keeps company with the Muses, then even whatever love of learning was in him, getting no taste of any study or inquiry or argument or culture, grows feeble and deaf and blind, since nothing wakes it or feeds it or clears its senses.'
'True,' he said.

'And such a man ends up hating reasoned argument and uncivilized, never using persuasion to get anything, but going at everything by brute force and fierceness, like a wild beast, living in ignorance and clumsiness, with no sense of measure or grace.'
'That's exactly right,' he said.

'So for these two parts of human nature, the spirited and the philosophic, some god, I'd say, has given men two arts to match them, music and physical training, and only incidentally for soul and body, so that the two parts may be tightened and slackened, like strings, until they're tuned to the proper pitch.'
'It does look that way,' he said.

'So the man who blends music and physical training in the finest proportion and applies them most measuredly to his soul, he's the one we'd rightly call truly musical and harmonious, far more than the man who merely tunes a lyre.'
'You're quite right, Socrates,' he said.
'And won't we always need someone like that to preside over our city, Glaucon, if its constitution is to last?'
'We'll need him more than anyone.'

'So much, then, for the patterns of upbringing and education. There's no need to go into every detail, the citizens' dances, their hunting and coursing, their athletic and equestrian contests. It's pretty clear that these follow from the principles we've laid down, and once we have the principles, working out the rest won't be hard.'
'No, it won't be hard,' he said.
'Good,' I said. 'Then what's the next question? Isn't it which of these men are to rule and which to be ruled?'
'It is.'
'And clearly the older must rule the younger.'
'Clearly.'
'And the best of the older must rule.'
'That too is clear.'
'Now, aren't the best farmers the ones most devoted to farming?'
'Yes.'
'So since we want the best of our guardians to rule, mustn't we pick the ones who have most the character of guardians of the city?'
'Yes.'
'And for that they need to be intelligent and capable, and to care for the city.'
'True.'
'And a man cares most for what he loves.'
'Necessarily.'
'And he loves a thing most when he believes its interests are the same as his own, and that when it does well or badly, he does well or badly with it.'
'Just so,' he said.

'So we'll have to pick out, from among the guardians, the kind of men who, all their lives, show the greatest eagerness to do whatever they think is good for the city, and the greatest unwillingness to do anything against it.'
'Those are the right men,' he said.

'And we'll have to watch them at every age, to see whether they hold on to this conviction and never, under the pull of force or enchantment, forget or throw off the belief that they must do what's best for the city.'
'What do you mean, throw off?' he said.
'I'll explain,' I said. 'A belief leaves a man's mind either willingly or unwillingly: willingly when he gives up a false belief and learns better, unwillingly whenever he loses a true one.'
'The willing loss I understand,' he said, 'but not the unwilling one.'

'Well, don't you think men lose good things against their will and bad things willingly? And isn't losing the truth a bad thing, and holding it a good one? And don't you agree that to hold the truth is to think things as they really are?'
'Yes,' he said. 'I agree that men are robbed of the truth against their will.'
'And doesn't this unwilling loss come about by theft, by force, or by enchantment?'
'Now I don't follow you again,' he said.

'I must be talking like a tragic poet,' I said. 'By those whose belief is stolen, I mean the ones who are talked out of it or who simply forget, argument quietly carrying it off from one set of men, time from the other. Now do you understand?'
'Yes.'
'And by those forced, I mean the ones whom some pain or grief compels to change their minds.'
'I understand that too,' he said, 'and you're right.'
'And the enchanted, I think you'd agree, are those who change their minds either under the gentler spell of pleasure or the harsher spell of fear.'
'Yes,' he said. 'Everything that deceives works a kind of enchantment.'

'So, as I was saying, we have to find out who are the best guardians of their own conviction that they must always do what they judge best for the city. We'll watch them from childhood and set them tasks in which a man would be most likely to forget such a conviction or be tricked out of it, and we'll pick the one who keeps it and isn't deceived, and reject the one who fails. Does that sound right?'
'Yes.'
'And we'll set them labors and pains and contests too, where they'll have to show the same qualities.'
'Quite right,' he said.

'And then,' I said, 'we'll test them with enchantments, that's the third kind of trial, and watch how they hold up. Just as colts are taken into noise and uproar to see whether they're skittish, we'll put our young men into terrors of some kind and then into pleasures, testing them harder than gold is tested in the fire, to see whether each stands proof against every enchantment, keeps his dignity throughout, guards himself well and guards the music he's learned, and shows himself, in all of it, rhythmical and harmonious, the kind of man most useful to himself and to the city. And the one who comes through the test pure, as boy and youth and grown man, we'll make a ruler and guardian of the city, and we'll honor him alive and dead, with the finest tombs and memorials we can give. The one who fails, we'll reject. That, I think, is roughly how our rulers and guardians should be chosen and appointed, in outline, without any claim to exactness.'
'In outline,' he said, 'I agree with you.'

'And perhaps it's truest to reserve the word "guardian" in its fullest sense for this higher class, the ones who protect us from enemies abroad and keep the peace among our citizens at home, so that the one group won't have the will to harm us and the other won't have the power. The younger men we were calling guardians we'd more properly call auxiliaries, the ones who support the rulers' decisions.'
'I agree,' he said.
'Now, how could we contrive one of those necessary lies we were talking about a while ago, a single noble lie that might convince even the rulers, or at least the rest of the city?'
'What sort of lie?' he said.

'Nothing new,' I said. 'An old Phoenician tale, the kind of thing that has happened before in many places, so the poets say and have persuaded men to believe, though it hasn't happened in our time, and I don't know whether it could happen again, or whether anyone could even be made to believe it.'
'How you hesitate to come out with it,' he said.
'You won't be surprised at my hesitation,' I said, 'once you've heard it.'
'Speak,' he said, 'and don't be afraid.'

'Then I'll speak, though I hardly know how to find the nerve, or the words, for so bold a fiction. I'll try to persuade first the rulers themselves, then the soldiers, and after them the rest of the city, that all the upbringing and education we gave them was a kind of dream, something they only seemed to undergo, while in reality, during all that time, they were being formed and raised deep within the earth, they themselves and their weapons and all their gear made down there. When they were finished, the earth, their mother, sent them up into the light. And so they must think of the land they live in as their mother and nurse, and defend her if anyone attacks her, and regard their fellow citizens as brothers, born of the same earth.'
'No wonder,' he said, 'you were ashamed to come out with your lie.'

'I had good reason,' I said. 'But there's more, so hear the rest. "You are all brothers in the city," we'll tell them in our tale, "but when the god fashioned you, he mixed gold into those of you fit to rule, which is why they're the most precious; silver into the auxiliaries; and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other craftsmen. Now, since you're all of one stock, you'll generally have children like yourselves, but sometimes a golden parent will have a silver child, or a silver parent a golden one, and so on through all the metals. So the god commands the rulers, before and above everything else, to be the finest guardians of nothing so much as the mixture of metals in their children's souls. If a child of theirs has bronze or iron in him, they must show no pity, but assign him the rank his nature deserves and push him out among the craftsmen or farmers. And if a child of those classes is born with gold or silver in him, they must honor him and raise him up to the guardians or the auxiliaries. For there's an oracle that the city will be destroyed on the day a man of iron or bronze becomes its guardian." That's the tale. Is there any way to make our citizens believe it?'
'No way at all,' he said, 'with these men. But their sons might believe it, and their sons' sons, and the generations after them.'

'I see the difficulty,' I said. 'Still, even that would make them care more for the city and for one another. But enough of the tale; let it fly abroad on rumor's wings. Let's arm these earthborn men of ours and lead them out under their commanders. Let them look about and pick the best spot in the city for a camp, one from which they can best keep down any rebellion within, if anyone refuses to obey, and best beat off enemies who might come down on the fold like wolves from outside. And once they've made their camp and sacrificed to the proper gods, let them see to their quarters.'
'Yes,' he said.
'And these quarters must be the kind that will shield them against winter's cold and summer's heat.'
'You mean houses, I suppose,' he said.
'Yes,' I said, 'but the houses of soldiers, not of moneymakers.'
'What's the difference?' he asked.

'I'll try to explain,' I said. 'Surely the most monstrous and shameful thing a shepherd could do would be to keep, as sheepdogs, dogs so badly disciplined, or so starved, or of such bad habits, that they'd turn on the sheep themselves and worry them like wolves instead of guarding them.'
'Monstrous indeed,' he said.
'So we have to take every care that our auxiliaries, being stronger than the other citizens, don't treat them like that, turning from friends and allies into savage masters.'
'Yes,' he said, 'great care.'
'And wouldn't a really good education be the best safeguard?'
'But they have it already,' he said.

'I wouldn't be so sure, my dear Glaucon,' I said. 'I'm surer of this: that they ought to have it, and that a true education, whatever it turns out to be, has the greatest power to make them gentle and humane toward one another and toward those in their care.'
'Very true,' he said.

'And besides their education, any man of sense would say their housing and everything else about their lives should be such as won't spoil their virtue as guardians or tempt them to prey on the other citizens.'
'He would,' he said.

'Then consider whether this is the way they must live and be housed, if they're to be the men we want. First, none of them should own any private property beyond what's absolutely necessary. None should have a house or storeroom that isn't open for anyone to enter. Their food should be the rations of disciplined warriors, self-controlled and brave, which they'll receive from the other citizens as the fixed wage of their guardianship, enough to cover the year with nothing left over. They'll dine together at common messes and live together like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, we'll tell them they have the divine kind always in their souls, given by the gods, and have no need of the human kind besides; that it would be sacrilege to defile their store of the divine metal by mixing it with mortal gold, since that common coin has been the cause of many unholy deeds, while their own is unalloyed. To them alone, of all the people in the city, it's forbidden to handle or touch gold or silver, to come under the same roof with it, to wear it as ornament, or to drink from cups of it. This will be their salvation, and the city's. But the moment they come to own land and houses and money of their own, they'll be householders and farmers instead of guardians, the other citizens' masters and enemies instead of their allies. They'll spend their whole lives hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, in far more fear of enemies within than of enemies without, themselves and the whole city racing toward ruin. For all these reasons, shall we say that this is how our guardians are to be housed and provided for, and lay it down as law?'
'Yes, by all means,' said Glaucon.
