sections.title: The Virtues of the City and the Soul

segments.text: Here Adeimantus broke in with a question. 'How would you answer, Socrates,' he said, 'if someone objected that you're making these men miserable, and that it's their own fault? The city really belongs to them, and yet they get nothing out of it. Other men buy up land, build big handsome houses, fill them with fine things, offer their own sacrifices to the gods, entertain guests, and on top of that own the gold and silver and everything else that goes with what people call good fortune. But your guardians might as well be hired mercenaries posted in the city with nothing to do but stand guard.'

'Yes,' I said, 'and you can add that they only get their keep, with no wages on top of their food the way other men have, so they can't even take a trip abroad if they wanted to, or spend on a mistress, or on any of the other luxuries that people think make for happiness. You could pile up a good many more charges of the same kind.'
'All right,' he said, 'let's count all of that as part of the accusation.'
'You want to know what our answer will be?' I said.
'Yes.'

'I think we'll find it if we keep to the road we've been on,' I said. 'Our answer will be this: it wouldn't surprise us if these men, even as they are, turned out to be the happiest of all. But that was never the point. When we founded the city, we weren't aiming to make any one class outstandingly happy. We were aiming at the greatest happiness of the city as a whole. We supposed that in a city ordered for the good of the whole we'd be most likely to find justice, and in a badly ordered one, injustice; and once we'd found them, we could decide which kind of life is the happier. Right now we're shaping the happy city, not by picking out a few people and making them happy, but as a whole. We'll look at the opposite kind of city later. Suppose we were painting a statue, and someone came up and complained, "Why don't you put the most beautiful colors on the most beautiful parts? The eyes are the finest feature, and you've painted them black instead of purple." We'd have a fair answer for him: "My friend, you wouldn't have us paint the eyes so beautifully that they stopped looking like eyes at all. Look instead at whether, by giving each part its proper color, we make the whole thing beautiful." So don't force us to give the guardians the kind of happiness that would turn them into anything but guardians. We could just as easily dress our farmers in fine robes and crowns of gold and tell them to work the land only when they felt like it; we could let our potters lie back on couches by the fire, passing the wine around, with the wheel beside them to turn whenever the mood took them. We could make every class happy that way, and then, as you imagine, the whole city would be happy. But don't put that idea into our heads. If we listened to you, the farmer would stop being a farmer, the potter would stop being a potter, and no one in the city would keep the character of his own role. With most trades it doesn't matter much. If shoemakers go soft and pretend to be what they're not, the city survives. But when the guardians of the laws and of the city only seem to be guardians and aren't, you can see how they'd bring the whole city to ruin, since they alone hold the power to govern it well and keep it happy. If we mean our guardians to be the true saviors of the city and not its destroyers, then the man who's objecting is thinking of peasants at a feast, enjoying a holiday, not of citizens doing their work in a city. So we're talking about two different things, and what he has in mind isn't a city at all. The question we have to settle, then, is whether in setting up our guardians we should aim at the greatest happiness of each of them taken alone, or whether we should look to the happiness of the city as a whole, and so compel or persuade these men, and all the others, to do their own work as well as it can be done. The whole city would then grow up in good order, and each class would get the share of happiness its nature allows.'
'I think you're quite right,' he said.
'I wonder whether you'll agree with something else that strikes me,' I said.
'What's that?'
'It seems to me there are two things that ruin a craft.'
'And what are they?'
'Wealth and poverty,' I said.
'How do they ruin it?'
'Like this,' I said. 'When a potter gets rich, do you suppose he'll still take the same care with his craft?'
'Certainly not.'
'He'll get lazier and more careless?'
'Much.'
'And so he'll become a worse potter?'
'Far worse.'
'But on the other hand, if he's so poor he can't even afford tools and the rest of his equipment, his own work will suffer, and he'll train his sons and apprentices to work just as badly.'
'Of course.'
'So under both, poverty and wealth, the craftsman's work declines, and so does the craftsman himself?'
'Plainly.'
'Then here's another pair of evils for the guardians to watch out for,' I said, 'and to keep from slipping into the city unnoticed.'
'What evils?'
'Wealth and poverty,' I said. 'The one breeds luxury and idleness and the urge to change things; the other breeds the same urge along with meanness and bad workmanship.'
'True,' he said. 'But here's something I'd like to understand, Socrates. How will our city manage to make war, if it has no money, especially against a rich and powerful enemy?'
'It would obviously be hard,' I said, 'against a single such enemy. Against two, it's easier.'
'How can that be?' he asked.
'In the first place,' I said, 'if it comes to a fight, won't our men be trained soldiers facing an army of rich men?'
'Yes, that's true,' he said.
'Well then, Adeimantus, don't you think a single boxer, in peak condition and trained in his art, could easily handle two well-fed gentlemen who don't know how to box?'
'Not if they both rushed him at once,' he said.

'What if he could give ground,' I said, 'and then turn and land a blow on whichever one came at him first, and do this again and again under a blazing sun? Couldn't a man like that, an expert, take down more than two of them?'
'No wonder if he did,' he said.
'And don't you think rich men have more skill and practice in boxing than they do in the art of war?'
'Probably,' he said.
'So our athletes will be able to fight two or three times their own number.'
'I'll grant you that. I think you're right.'

'And suppose, before fighting, our men sent envoys to one of the two enemy cities to tell them the simple truth: "We have no silver or gold and we're not even allowed to have any, but you are. Come fight on our side, and you can keep the spoils of the other city." Who, hearing that, would choose to fight lean, wiry dogs rather than join the dogs against fat, soft sheep?'
'No one would,' he said. 'Still, if all that wealth got gathered into a single city, that might be dangerous for the poor one.'
'How naive of you,' I said, 'to call any of them a city but ours!'
'What do you mean?'

'You should use the plural for the others,' I said, 'because none of them is one city. Each is many cities, like the cities on a game board. At the very least, any city, however small, is really two cities at war with each other, the city of the poor and the city of the rich, and within each of those are many more divisions. Treat them as one and you'll miss the mark completely. But treat them as many, and offer the wealth or power or people of one faction to another, and you'll always have plenty of allies and few enemies. And as long as our city holds to the wise order we've laid down, it will be the greatest of cities. I don't mean greatest in reputation, but in fact and in truth, even if its fighting men number no more than a thousand. You won't easily find a single city to match it, Greek or barbarian, though plenty look as great, and many times greater.'
'That's perfectly true,' he said.
'And what,' I said, 'is the best limit for our rulers to set when they decide how large the city should be, and how much territory to take in, before they stop?'
'What limit would you propose?' he asked.
'I'd let the city grow as far as it can without losing its unity,' I said, 'and no further. That, I think, is the right limit.'
'Good,' he said.
'So here's another order for our guardians,' I said. 'See to it that the city is neither large nor small, but one and self-sufficient.'
'That's hardly a hard order to lay on them,' he said.

'And here's one even lighter,' I said, 'the one I mentioned before, that if a guardian's child turns out inferior, it should be sent down to the other classes, and if a child of the lower classes turns out naturally superior, it should be raised up among the guardians. The point was that each citizen should be put to the single work that suits his nature, so that, by doing his own one thing, each man becomes one and not many, and the whole city likewise becomes one and not many.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's not so hard either.'

'My good Adeimantus,' I said, 'these rules we're laying down aren't, as you might think, a long list of grand principles. They're all trivial, provided we take care, as the saying goes, of the one great thing, though I'd rather not call it great, only sufficient.'
'And what is that?' he asked.

'Education and upbringing,' I said. 'If our citizens are well educated and grow into sensible men, they'll see their own way through all of this easily enough, and through everything I'm leaving out too, like marriage, and the having of wives, and the bearing of children, all of which should follow the principle that, as the proverb says, friends hold everything in common.'
'That would be the best way to arrange it,' he said.

'And once a city gets a good start,' I said, 'it gathers momentum like a turning wheel. A good upbringing and education breed good natures, and good natures, taking in turn a good education, grow better still, in people as in the other animals.'
'Very likely,' he said.

'So, to sum up, this is what our rulers must guard above everything: that education in music and physical training is kept from being tampered with, and not the slightest change made. They must do all they can to preserve it as it is. And when someone praises a song by saying that what people most prize is "the newest song the singers have," they should be afraid he's praising not new songs but a new kind of music, which is not what the poet meant and should not be praised. To bring in a new kind of music is to risk the whole city, and it should be forbidden. So Damon says, and I believe him: when the modes of music change, the fundamental laws of the city always change with them.'
'Count me in too,' said Adeimantus, 'on the side of Damon and yourself.'
'Then our guardians,' I said, 'must build the outpost of their defense here, in music.'
'Yes,' he said, 'lawlessness slips in there all too easily.'
'It does,' I said, 'in the form of play, where at first it looks harmless.'

'And it would be harmless,' he said, 'except that little by little it settles in and quietly works its way into people's manners and habits. From there it spills, stronger now, into their dealings with one another, and from their dealings it moves on, recklessly, into the laws and the constitution, until in the end, Socrates, it overturns everything, public and private alike.'
'Is that so?' I said.
'I believe it,' he said.

'Then as I was saying, our young people must be brought up from the start under a stricter discipline. For if their play becomes lawless, and they grow up lawless along with it, they can never become law-abiding, serious men.'
'True,' he said.

'But when children begin their play in the right way and take in good order through music, then, unlike the lawless children, that orderliness goes with them in everything they do, and makes them grow. And if anything in the city has fallen into decay, men like these will set it right again.'
'Very true,' he said.
'Men brought up this way,' I said, 'will rediscover for themselves even the small customs that their predecessors let drop.'
'Which ones do you mean?'

'Things like these,' I said. 'When the young should keep silent before their elders, how they should give up their seats and stand to show respect, how they should care for their parents, how they wear their hair and what clothes and shoes they put on, their whole bearing, and so forth. Don't you agree?'
'I do.'
'But I think it would be foolish to make laws about such things. They never really stick that way, and no written rule about them is likely to last.'
'It couldn't,' he said.
'It seems, Adeimantus,' I said, 'that the direction a person is started off in by his education shapes everything that comes after. Doesn't like always call out to like?'
'It does.'
'And it leads, I suppose, to some single decisive outcome, for good or for the opposite of good?'
'No doubt,' he said.
'So for my part,' I said, 'I wouldn't try to legislate any further about these small matters.'
'And reasonably so,' he said.

'Well then, what about the business of the marketplace, the ordinary dealings between one man and another, and the contracts with craftsmen, the cases of slander and assault and the filing of lawsuits, the seating of juries, and any duties that have to be paid or collected at the market or the harbor, and the regulation of markets and harbors and the city police, and all the rest of it? Should we really stoop to making laws about any of these?'
'There's no need to dictate such laws to good men,' he said. 'They'll find out for themselves easily enough whatever rules are needed.'
'Yes, my friend,' I said, 'provided a god grants them the survival of the laws we've already given.'
'Otherwise,' said Adeimantus, 'they'll spend their lives endlessly passing laws and amending them, always thinking they're about to reach perfection.'
'You make them sound,' I said, 'like sick men too undisciplined to give up a way of life that's bad for them.'
'Exactly.'
'And what a charming life they lead!' I said. 'They doctor themselves and only make the trouble worse and more complicated, forever hoping that some new remedy somebody recommends will cure them.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's just how it goes with that kind of invalid.'

'And the delightful part,' I said, 'is that they treat as their worst enemy anyone who tells them the plain truth, which is that until they stop their drinking and overeating and womanizing and idleness, no drug or cautery or charm or amulet will do them any good.'
'There's nothing charming about it,' he said. 'There's nothing pleasant in flying into a rage at a man who tells you what's right.'
'You don't seem to think much of these people,' I said.
'I certainly don't.'

'Then you won't praise a whole city that behaves the same way. Aren't there badly governed cities that warn their citizens, on pain of death, not to disturb the established order, and yet the man who serves that order most sweetly, who flatters and indulges and panders to it, anticipating its every whim and gratifying it, is held up as a great man and a fine statesman? Don't such cities behave just like those sick men?'
'They do,' he said. 'I have no praise for them at all.'
'But what about the men who eagerly serve such cities? Don't you admire their nerve and their cleverness?'
'I do,' he said, 'except for the ones the crowd's applause has fooled into thinking they're real statesmen. Those I can't admire.'

'What do you mean?' I said. 'Have a little sympathy. When a man can't measure, and a crowd of others who can't measure either keep telling him he's six feet tall, how is he supposed to help believing it?'
'No,' he said, 'in that case he can't.'

'Then don't be angry with them. They're as good as a comedy, these men, with their petty reforms of the kind I was describing. They keep imagining that by passing laws they'll put an end to fraud in contracts and all the other rackets I mentioned, never realizing that they're really just lopping the heads off a hydra.'
'That's exactly what they're doing,' he said.

'So I'd say the true lawmaker shouldn't bother with this class of laws and constitutional details, in a badly run city or a well-run one. In the badly run city they're useless, and in the well-run one some of them anyone can figure out, while the rest follow naturally from what we've already laid down.'
'Then what's left of the work of legislation for us?' he asked.
'For us, nothing,' I said. 'But for Apollo, the god at Delphi, there remain the greatest and finest and most important laws of all.'
'And which are those?' he asked.

'The founding of temples, the sacrifices, and the whole service of the gods, the spirits, and the heroes; and likewise the burial of the dead and all the rites we owe the powers of the world below to keep them favorable. These are things we don't understand ourselves, and in founding a city we'd be unwise to trust them to any guide but our ancestral one. And this god, seated at the center of the earth, on its very navel, is the ancestral guide who interprets such things for all mankind.'
'Well said,' he replied. 'And that's what we'll do.'

'So now,' I said, 'son of Ariston, our city has been founded and made fit to live in. Bring a light and search it, and call in your brother and Polemarchus and the rest, and let's see if we can spot somewhere in it where justice lies and where injustice, how they differ from each other, and which of the two the man who means to be happy must have, whether gods and men see him have it or not.'
'Nonsense,' said Glaucon. 'You promised to do the searching yourself. You said it would be an act of impiety to fail to come to justice's aid when you could.'
'You're right, I did say that,' I replied, 'and since you remind me, I'll keep my word. But you'll have to help.'
'We will,' he said.
'Then here's how I hope to find it,' I said. 'I'll start from the assumption that our city, if it's been rightly founded, is completely good.'
'It must be,' he said.
'And if it's completely good, then it's wise and brave and temperate and just.'
'Clearly.'
'Then if we find some of these qualities in it, whatever's left over will be the one we haven't yet found?'
'Of course.'

'Suppose there were four things in something, and we were looking for one of them. If we spotted the one we wanted first, that would settle it. But if we recognized the other three first, that would settle it too, since the one we were after would obviously be the one left over.'
'True,' he said.
'And since the virtues we're looking for also happen to be four, don't we follow the same method?'
'Plainly.'
'Well, the first of them I think I can see in the city is wisdom, and there's something peculiar about it.'
'What's that?'
'The city we've described is called wise, I take it, because it's sound in its deliberations?'
'Yes.'
'And sound deliberation is clearly a kind of knowledge. Men deliberate well by knowledge, not by ignorance.'
'Obviously.'
'But there are many different kinds of knowledge in a city.'
'Of course.'
'Is it because of the carpenters' knowledge, then, that we call the city wise and well-advised?'
'Not at all,' he said. 'That would only make it good at carpentry.'
'So a city isn't called wise because of the knowledge that gives the best advice about wooden furniture?'
'No.'
'And not because of knowledge about bronze ware, or any knowledge of that sort?'
'None of those,' he said.
'And not because of the knowledge of how to grow crops from the soil? That would only make it good at farming.'
'I think so.'

'Well then,' I said, 'is there some knowledge, in this city we've just founded, possessed by some of its citizens, that advises not about any one particular thing in the city but about the city as a whole, how it should best conduct itself toward itself and toward other cities?'
'There certainly is.'
'And what is that knowledge,' I asked, 'and who has it?'
'It's the knowledge of the guardians,' he said, 'found in those we called the perfect guardians.'
'And what name do we give the city because it has this knowledge?'
'Sound in counsel,' he said, 'and truly wise.'
'And do you think there'll be more of these true guardians in our city, or more metalworkers?'
'Far more metalworkers,' he said.
'And of all the groups that get a name from the kind of knowledge they have, won't the guardians be the smallest of all?'
'Much the smallest.'

'So it's because of the smallest part of itself, and the knowledge in the part that presides and rules, that the whole city, founded according to nature, is wise. And this part, which alone has the knowledge that deserves to be called wisdom, is by nature the smallest of all.'
'Perfectly true,' he said.
'So there it is. One of the four, somehow or other, we've found, both what it is and where in the city it sits.'
'And found it well enough to satisfy me,' he said.
'Now courage,' I said, 'is no harder to make out, both the quality itself and the part of the city in which it sits and gives the city its name.'
'How do you mean?'
'Anyone who calls a city brave or cowardly,' I said, 'will be thinking of the part that fights and goes to war on the city's behalf.'
'No one,' he said, 'would think of anyone else.'
'I'd say the rest of the citizens can be as brave or as cowardly as you like, and it won't make the city itself one or the other.'
'No.'

'A city is brave, then, by a part of itself, the part that holds onto, through everything, the right belief about what is to be feared and what isn't, the belief the lawmaker instilled in their education. That, I take it, is what you call courage.'
'I'd like to hear that again,' he said. 'I don't think I quite followed.'
'I'm saying that courage is a kind of preservation,' I said.
'Preservation of what?'

'Of the belief, planted by the law through education, about what things are to be feared and what their nature is. And by saying "through everything" I mean holding onto that belief and never letting go of it, whether under the pull of pleasure or pain, of desire or fear. Shall I give you a comparison?'
'Please.'

'You know how dyers work,' I said. 'When they want to dye wool a true sea-purple, they first pick out the white wool from all the rest, then prepare and treat it with great care so it will take the dye in full, and only then dip it. Whatever is dyed that way takes a fast color, and no washing, with or without soap, can strip the brightness out of it. But if the wool isn't prepared first, you know what happens, whether they use purple or any other color.'
'Yes,' he said, 'it comes out washed-out and ridiculous.'

'Then you'll see what we were trying to do when we chose our soldiers and trained them in music and physical exercise. We were working out how to get them to take the dye of the laws as thoroughly as possible, so that their belief about what to fear, and every other belief, would be fixed fast by their upbringing and training, and no soap, no matter how strong, would wash it out, not pleasure, which is a more powerful solvent of the soul than any soda or lye, and not pain or fear or desire either, the strongest solvents of all. This power to hold onto, through everything, the right and lawful belief about what is and isn't to be feared, this is what I call courage, unless you object.'
'I don't object,' he said. 'I take it you mean to exclude the raw, untaught courage of a wild animal or a slave. That, in your view, isn't lawful courage and ought to have some other name.'
'Exactly right,' I said.
'Then I accept that this is courage.'

'Accept it,' I said, 'at least as the courage of a citizen, and you won't be far wrong. We'll come back to it later and go into it more fully if you like, but for now we're after justice, not courage, and we've said enough for that.'
'Fair enough,' he said.
'Two virtues are left to find in the city,' I said, 'temperance, and then justice, which is the whole point of our search.'
'True.'
'Now, could we somehow get to justice without bothering with temperance?'
'I don't see how,' he said, 'and I wouldn't want justice brought to light at the cost of leaving temperance in the dark. So please, do me the favor of taking up temperance first.'
'I could hardly refuse you,' I said.
'Then go ahead,' he said.
'I will,' I said. 'And as far as I can see at this point, temperance is more like a harmony, a tuning, than the two before it.'
'How so?' he asked.

'Temperance,' I said, 'is a kind of order and a mastery over certain pleasures and desires. People hint at this when they call a man, in that odd phrase, "master of himself," and there are other traces of the same idea scattered through the way we talk.'
'No doubt,' he said.

'But isn't "master of himself" a ridiculous phrase? If he's master of himself, then he's also slave to himself, and if he's slave to himself, master of himself, since it's the same man we're talking about throughout.'
'Of course.'

'What the phrase means, I think, is that within the same person, in his soul, there's a better part and a worse part, and when the part that's naturally better controls the worse, we say the man is master of himself, as a kind of praise. But when, through a bad upbringing or bad company, the better part, which is also the smaller, is swamped by the larger mass of the worse, then we reproach the man and call him a slave to himself and undisciplined.'
'And rightly,' he said.

'Now look at our newly founded city,' I said, 'and you'll find one of these two conditions in it. You'll agree it can fairly be called master of itself, if a thing in which the better part rules the worse deserves to be called temperate and master of itself.'
'I'm looking,' he said, 'and what you say is true.'
'And the many complicated pleasures and pains and desires you'll find mostly in children and women and slaves, and in the great majority of so-called free men, the lowest sort.'
'Certainly.'
'While the simple, moderate desires, the ones guided by reasoning and by right belief and intelligence, you'll find in only a few, those born with the best natures and given the best education.'
'True.'
'And don't you see both of these in our city, with the desires of the worse and more numerous part held in check by the desires and the wisdom of the better and fewer?'
'I do,' he said.
'So if any city deserves to be called master of its own pleasures and desires, and master of itself, ours does.'
'It does indeed,' he said.
'And temperate too, for the same reasons?'
'Yes.'
'And if there's any city in which the rulers and the ruled agree about who should rule, it's ours.'
'Beyond a doubt.'
'And with the citizens in such agreement, in which group will temperance reside, the rulers or the ruled?'
'In both, I'd say,' he replied.
'You see we weren't far off,' I said, 'when we guessed temperance was a kind of harmony.'
'How do you mean?'

'Because, unlike courage and wisdom, each of which sat in one part of the city and made it brave or wise, temperance isn't like that. It stretches across the whole, making the weakest and the strongest and those in between all sing the same note, whether you rank them by intelligence, or strength, or numbers, or wealth, or anything else. So we'd be quite right to call temperance this agreement, this harmony between the naturally worse and the naturally better about which of them should rule, in a city or in a single man.'
'I agree completely,' he said.
'Good,' I said. 'So three of the four are in view in our city. What's the last kind, the one that makes a city good? Clearly it must be justice.'
'Clearly.'

'So now, Glaucon, like hunters, we have to surround the thicket and keep a sharp watch so justice doesn't slip away and vanish on us. She's in here somewhere, no doubt about it. So look hard, strain to catch sight of her, and if you spot her first, give me the word.'
'I wish I could,' he said. 'But really you should treat me as a follower, someone with just enough sight to make out whatever you point to. That's about all I'm good for.'
'Then say a prayer with me,' I said, 'and follow.'
'I will,' he said, 'only lead the way.'
'There's no path here,' I said, 'and the wood is dark and hard to see through. Still, we have to push on.'
'Then let's push on,' he said.
And just then I caught something. 'Look!' I cried. 'I think I see a track. I believe the quarry won't get away from us after all.'
'Good news,' he said.
'We really are slow-witted,' I said.
'How so?'

'My good man, it's been right under our feet from the start, ages ago, tumbling about there in front of us, and we never saw it. Nothing could be more absurd. It's like people hunting all over for something they're already holding in their hand. We kept staring off into the distance instead of at the thing in front of us, and that's probably how we missed it.'
'What do you mean?' he said.
'I mean that all this time, I think, we've been talking about justice and saying what it is without realizing that's what we were doing.'
'I'm getting impatient with this long preamble,' he said.

'Then tell me whether I'm right,' I said. 'You remember the principle we kept coming back to from the very founding of the city, that each man should do the one thing his nature best suits him for. Well, justice is that principle, or a part of it.'
'Yes, we kept saying each man should do one thing.'
'And we said, again and again, that justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in other people's. Plenty of others have said the same.'
'We did say that.'
'Then it seems, my friend, that doing one's own work, in a certain way, is justice. Do you know what makes me think so?'
'No, tell me.'

'I think it's because this is the one thing left over in the city once we've set aside the others we examined, temperance, courage, and wisdom. It's what made all of those possible in the first place, and once they're there it keeps them safe as long as it stays in them. And we did say that if we found the other three, justice would be the one remaining.'
'That follows of necessity,' he said.

'Now, if we had to decide which of these four does most, by being present, to make the city good, it wouldn't be easy. Is it the agreement of rulers and ruled? Or the soldiers' preservation of the lawful belief about what's truly to be feared? Or the wisdom and watchfulness in the rulers? Or is it this other thing, present in child and woman, slave and free, craftsman, ruler, and ruled, the doing of one's own single work and not meddling? Which deserves the prize? It's hard to say.'
'It is,' he said.
'So this power, each man in the city doing his own work, seems to compete with the other three virtues, wisdom and temperance and courage, for making the city good.'
'It does,' he said.
'And we'd call this competing virtue justice?'
'Exactly.'
'Look at it another way, and see if you agree. Won't you assign your rulers the job of judging lawsuits?'
'Of course.'
'And when they judge, what will they aim at but this, that no one take what belongs to another or be deprived of his own?'
'Yes, that's the principle.'
'Because that's just?'
'Yes.'
'So on this view too, justice turns out to be the having and doing of what is one's own and belongs to one.'
'That's right.'

'Now see whether you agree with this. Suppose a carpenter set about doing the shoemaker's work, or the shoemaker the carpenter's, and they swapped their tools and their jobs, or suppose one man tried to do both at once. Would the city take much harm from that?'
'Not much,' he said.

'But suppose a man who's a craftsman by nature, or some other money-maker, gets puffed up by his wealth or his strength or the number of his supporters, and tries to force his way into the soldier class, or a soldier into the class of the rulers and guardians when he isn't fit for it, and they trade their tools and their jobs around; or suppose one man tries to do all of these at once. I think you'll agree that this swapping and meddling among the three classes is the ruin of the city.'
'Absolutely.'
'So the meddling and exchange among these three classes is the greatest harm to the city, and we'd be most justified in calling it the worst of crimes against it.'
'Just so.'
'And the worst crime against one's own city, wouldn't you call that injustice?'
'Of course.'
'So this is injustice. And turn it around: when the money-making class, the soldiers, and the guardians each do their own work in the city, that is justice, and it makes the city just.'
'I'd say that's exactly so,' he said.

'Let's not be too sure just yet,' I said. 'If this idea of justice holds good when we apply it to the individual man as well as the city, we'll grant it; there'll be nothing more to say. But if it doesn't fit the individual, we'll have to look again. First, let's finish what we set out to do. We took it that if we examined justice on the larger scale first, in something bigger that has it, we'd find it easier to make out in the single man. The city seemed to be that larger thing, so we built the best one we could, sure that justice would be found in a good city. Now let's carry over what we found there to the individual. If it matches, good. If the individual shows us something different, we'll go back to the city and test the idea again. Maybe, by rubbing the two cases together like fire-sticks, we'll make justice flash out, and once we've seen it we can fix it firmly in our minds.'
'That's the right way to go about it,' he said. 'Let's do as you say.'
'Now,' I said, 'when you call two things by the same name, one larger and one smaller, are they alike or unlike in respect of the thing the name refers to?'
'Alike,' he said.
'So the just man, in respect of justice itself, won't differ at all from the just city; he'll be like it.'
'He will,' he said.

'And we decided a city is just when each of its three kinds of nature does its own work, and that it's temperate and brave and wise because of certain other conditions and states of those same three.'
'True.'
'So we'll expect the individual to have these same three kinds in his soul, and to deserve the same names as the city because he's in the same conditions as it is.'
'That must be so,' he said.
'Once again, then, my friend, we've stumbled into an easy little question about the soul, whether it has these three kinds in it or not.'
'It doesn't look so easy to me,' he said. 'But maybe the proverb's right, Socrates, that fine things are hard.'

'Apparently,' I said. 'And I'll tell you frankly, Glaucon, that in my opinion we'll never get a precise answer to this by the methods we've been using. The road that leads there is another and a longer one. Still, we may reach an answer that's up to the standard of what we've already said.'
'Won't that do?' he said. 'For now it would satisfy me.'
'And me,' I said.
'Then don't give up,' he said. 'Press on with the inquiry.'

'Well,' I said, 'we have to admit, don't we, that each of us has in himself the very same kinds and characters that are in the city? Where else could the city have got them from? It would be absurd to think that the spirited, high-tempered quality came to be in a city from any source but the individuals who have it, the people we credit with it, the Thracians and Scythians and the northern peoples generally. Or take the love of learning, which one might especially credit to our part of the world, or the love of money, which you could fairly attribute to the Phoenicians and the Egyptians.'
'Exactly,' he said.
'So this much is plain enough,' I said.
'Quite plain.'

'But here's where it gets harder. Do we do each of these with the same part of ourselves, or with three different parts? Do we learn with one part, get angry with another, and with a third desire the pleasures of food and sex and the like, or do we do each of these with the whole soul? That's what's hard to settle.'
'I agree,' he said. 'That's the difficulty.'
'Then let's try this way to decide whether they're the same or different.'
'How?' he asked.

'It's clear,' I said, 'that the same thing can't do or undergo opposite things in the same respect and in relation to the same thing at the same time. So if we find that happening here, we'll know we're dealing not with one thing but with more than one.'
'All right.'
'Take this case. Can the same thing be at rest and in motion at the same time, in the same part of itself?'
'Of course not.'

'Let's be even more precise, so we don't fall out over words later. If someone said of a man who's standing still but moving his hands and his head that the same man is both at rest and in motion at once, we wouldn't accept that way of speaking. We'd say one part of him is at rest and another in motion.'
'True.'

'And if our objector got cleverer still and pointed out that a spinning top, whirling with its point fixed in one spot, is at rest and in motion as a whole at the same time, and said the same of anything that turns in place, we wouldn't accept it, because such things aren't at rest and in motion in the same part of themselves. We'd say they have an axis and a circumference; with respect to the axis they're at rest, since they don't lean off it, and with respect to the circumference they're moving. But if the axis itself tips to the right or left, forward or back, while it spins, then it's not at rest in any respect.'
'And we'd be right to say so,' he replied.
'So no objection of that kind will throw us off or persuade us that one and the same thing could ever, in the same respect and toward the same thing, at the same time, do or undergo opposites.'
'It won't, not as far as I'm concerned,' he said.

'Still,' I said, 'so we don't have to wade through every such objection and prove each one false, let's assume this principle is sound and go ahead, agreeing that if it ever turns out to be false, everything we build on it falls with it.'
'That's the best way,' he said.

'Now then,' I said, 'wouldn't you put nodding yes and shaking the head no, reaching for something and pushing it away, drawing toward and thrusting off, all in the class of opposites, whether they're things you do or things done to you? That makes no difference to their being opposites.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they're opposites.'

'And what about thirst and hunger, and the desires generally, and willing and wishing? Wouldn't you put all of those somewhere among the things we just mentioned? Wouldn't you say the soul of a man who desires is reaching for the thing it desires, drawing toward itself what it wants to have, or that, insofar as it wills something to be given to it, it nods yes to itself, longing for that, as if someone had asked it a question?'
'I would.'
'And not-willing, refusing, not desiring, wouldn't we put those with the soul's pushing away and thrusting off, the opposite class?'
'Of course.'
'That being so, let's say there's a class of desires, and the clearest of them are the ones we call thirst and hunger.'
'Let's say so,' he said.
'And one of these is for drink, the other for food?'
'Yes.'

'Now, insofar as it's thirst, is it a desire in the soul for anything more than what we said, for drink? Is thirst, just as thirst, a thirst for hot drink or cold, for much or little, for any particular kind of drink at all? Or is it that if heat goes along with the thirst, that adds the desire for something cold, and if cold, for something hot; and if the thirst is great because of some added largeness, the desire is for much, and if small, for little? But thirst itself will never be a desire for anything but its natural object, drink, just as hunger is for food.'
'That's right,' he said. 'Each desire, in itself, is just for its own natural object, and the desire for a particular kind of thing comes from something added on.'

'Let's be careful here,' I said, 'so that no one catches us off guard with the objection that no one desires drink as such, but good drink, or food as such, but good food, since everyone desires good things, and so, thirst being a desire, it must be a desire for good drink, and the same with every other desire.'
'There might be something to that objection,' he said.

'But surely,' I said, 'with things that are relative to something, the qualified ones are relative to a qualified object, while the thing taken by itself is relative only to its object taken by itself.'
'I don't follow,' he said.
'You understand that the greater is what it is in relation to the less?'
'Certainly.'
'And the much greater to the much less?'
'Yes.'
'And the once-greater to the once-less, and the going-to-be-greater to the going-to-be-less?'
'Of course,' he said.
'And so with more in relation to fewer, double to half, and all such pairs, and heavier to lighter, faster to slower, and again hot to cold, and everything of that kind?'
'Yes.'

'And isn't it the same with the branches of knowledge? Knowledge as such is knowledge of what can be learned, or whatever we should call its object, while a particular knowledge of a particular kind is knowledge of a particular object. Take the building of houses: it's a kind of knowledge, marked off from the others, and so it's called architecture.'
'Certainly.'
'And it's called that because it has a particular character that none of the others has?'
'Yes.'
'And it has that character because it has an object of a particular kind, and the same goes for all the other arts and branches of knowledge?'
'It does.'

'Well then,' I said, 'take that as what I meant before about relatives, if you understand me now. I meant that whenever one term is taken just by itself, it's relative to its object just by itself, and whenever it's qualified, to a qualified object. I'm not saying it's relative to an object of its own kind, that knowledge of health is itself healthy or knowledge of disease diseased, or that knowledge of good and bad is itself good or bad. I'm only saying that once knowledge becomes knowledge not of its object as such but of a qualified object, in this case of health and disease, it gets a particular character itself, and so it's no longer called just knowledge but, with the qualification added, medicine.'
'I understand,' he said, 'and I think you're right.'
'And thirst, won't you put it among the things that are relative to something, being what it is in relation to something?'
'I will,' he said. 'Thirst is relative to drink.'
'So a particular kind of thirst is for a particular kind of drink, but thirst itself isn't for much or little, good or bad, or any particular kind of drink at all, but simply for drink itself.'
'Absolutely.'
'So the soul of the thirsty man, insofar as he's thirsty, wants nothing but to drink. That's what it reaches for and strains toward.'
'Plainly.'

'Then if something ever pulls it back when it's thirsty, that must be something in it different from the thirsty part, the part that drives it like a beast to drink. For we agreed the same thing can't, with the same part of itself, at the same time, in relation to the same object, do opposite things.'
'No, it can't.'
'Just as you wouldn't say the archer's hands push the bow away and draw it in at the same time, but that one hand pushes and the other pulls.'
'Exactly,' he said.
'Now, can a man be thirsty and yet unwilling to drink?'
'Yes,' he said, 'that happens all the time.'
'And what should we say about that? Isn't there something in his soul telling him to drink, and something else, different, holding him back, something that overrules the part that's telling him to?'
'I think so,' he said.
'And doesn't the part that holds him back, when it holds him back, come from reasoning, while the part that drives and drags him comes from feelings and from disorders of the body?'
'It seems so.'

'So we'd be right to judge them two distinct things,' I said. 'The part of the soul by which it reasons we'll call the rational part; the part by which it lusts and hungers and thirsts and is stirred by the other desires, the irrational and appetitive part, the companion of certain satisfactions and pleasures.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's a fair way to think of it.'

'Then let's take it as settled that these two parts exist in the soul. Now, what about the spirited part, the part by which we feel anger? Is it a third, or is it the same in nature as one of these two?'
'It might be the same as the appetitive part,' he said.

'There's a story I once heard,' I said, 'and I believe it. Leontius, the son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus, along the outside of the north wall, when he saw the public executioner's corpses lying there. He wanted to look at them and at the same time was disgusted and turned himself away. For a while he fought with himself and covered his eyes, but in the end his desire got the better of him, and he ran over to the bodies, forcing his eyes wide open and crying, "There, curse you, feast yourselves on the lovely sight!"'
'I've heard that story too,' he said.
'And its point,' I said, 'is that anger sometimes makes war on the desires, as though it were one thing and they were another.'
'That is the point,' he said.

'And don't we notice, in plenty of other cases, that when a man's desires force him against his reasoning, he rails at himself and his anger rises against the part of him that's forcing him? It's as if there were two factions at war, and his spirit takes the side of his reason. But when his spirit sides with the desires against what reason has decided shouldn't be done, that's a thing I think you've never noticed happening in yourself, or, I'd guess, in anyone else.'
'No, never,' he said.

'And take a man who believes he's done wrong. The finer his nature, the less he's able to feel anger when he suffers hunger or cold or any other pain at the hands of the man he wronged, because he thinks it's deserved. His spirit, as I say, refuses to rouse itself against it.'
'True,' he said.

'But when a man believes he's the one being wronged, then his spirit boils and rages and fights on the side of what he takes to be just. Through hunger and cold and every other suffering it holds out and wins, and his noble spirit won't be quieted until it has either won through or died, or until, like a dog called off by its shepherd, it is called back and calmed by the reason within him.'
'A perfect comparison,' he said. 'And it fits what we said about our city, that the auxiliaries were to be like dogs, obeying the rulers, who are like the shepherds of the city.'
'You understand me exactly,' I said. 'But there's one more thing to consider.'
'What's that?'

'That the spirited part has turned out to be the opposite of what we just thought. We supposed it was a kind of desire, but now we say that, in the soul's civil war, it takes up arms on the side of reason.'
'Definitely,' he said.

'But is it then different from reason as well, or only a kind of reason? In that case there wouldn't be three parts of the soul but two, the rational and the appetitive. Or just as the city was held together by three classes, the money-makers, the auxiliaries, and the rulers, is there in the soul too this third thing, the spirited part, the natural helper of reason, as long as it hasn't been ruined by a bad upbringing?'
'There must be a third,' he said.
'Yes,' I said, 'provided it turns out to be distinct from reason, just as we showed it was distinct from desire.'

'That's easy to show,' he said. 'You can see it in small children. They're full of spirit from the moment they're born, while some of them, in my view, never come to reason at all, and most do so only late.'

'A fine point,' I said. 'And you can see the same in animals, which is further proof of what you say. And we can call again on the line of Homer we quoted before, where he says, "He struck his breast and rebuked his heart." There Homer clearly treats the part that reasons about better and worse as different from the part that feels unreasoning anger and is rebuked by it.'
'Exactly right,' he said.
'So,' I said, 'after a hard swim we've reached land, and we're fairly agreed that the same three kinds are in the soul that are in the city.'
'Just so.'
'Then doesn't it follow at once that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same part that makes the city wise?'
'Certainly.'
'And that the part that makes the individual brave is the same that makes the city brave, and so on, the individual matching the city in every virtue?'
'It must be so.'
'And we'll say a man is just, Glaucon, in the same way the city is just.'
'That follows too, of course.'
'And we haven't forgotten that the city was just because each of its three classes did its own work?'
'I don't think we've forgotten,' he said.
'Then we must keep in mind that each of us, too, will be just, and do his own work, when each of the parts in him does its own.'
'Yes,' he said, 'we must keep that in mind.'
'And isn't it for the rational part, since it is wise and looks after the whole soul, to rule, and for the spirited part to be its subject and its ally?'
'Certainly.'

'And, as we said, won't the blend of music and physical training bring these two into accord, tightening and feeding the reason with fine words and learning, and loosening, soothing, and taming the spirited part with harmony and rhythm?'
'Just so,' he said.

'And these two, so nourished and truly taught their own work, will govern the appetitive part, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature the greediest for money. They'll watch it closely, in case it grows fat and strong on the so-called pleasures of the body and stops keeping to its own work, and tries instead to enslave and rule the parts it has no business ruling, and so wrecks the whole life of the man.'
'Quite so,' he said.

'And wouldn't these two be the best guardians of the whole soul and the whole body against enemies from outside, the one taking counsel, the other doing battle, following its ruler and carrying out by its courage what reason decides?'
'Yes.'
'And we call a man brave, I think, when his spirited part holds onto what reason declares is and isn't to be feared, through pleasure and through pain alike.'
'Rightly,' he said.

'And we call him wise by that small part of him that rules and gives those declarations, the part that has in it the knowledge of what's good for each of the three parts and for the whole they make together.'
'Certainly.'
'And don't we call him temperate by the friendship and harmony of these same parts, when the ruler and the two ruled agree that the rational part should rule and don't make war on it?'
'That's exactly what temperance is,' he said, 'in a city or in a man.'
'And of course a man will be just by what we've now said so many times, and in the way we've said.'
'Necessarily.'
'Now,' I said, 'is justice in the individual any blurrier than it was in the city? Does it come out as something different there, or the same?'
'The same, I'd say,' he replied.
'Because, if any doubt is still hanging in our minds, we can settle it for certain with a few ordinary examples.'
'What sort of examples?'

'Suppose someone asked us about that just city and a man brought up in its spirit, whether such a man would embezzle a deposit of gold or silver entrusted to him. Who would think he'd be more likely to do it than men of the other sort?'
'No one,' he said.
'And wouldn't such a man be the last to commit temple-robbery, or theft, or betrayal, whether of his friends in private or of his city in public?'
'He would.'
'And he'd never be faithless to an oath or any other agreement?'
'How could he?'
'And adultery, neglect of his parents, failure in his religious duties, no one would be less likely to fall into any of these than he.'
'No one,' he said.
'And isn't the reason for all this that each part of him is doing its own work, in ruling and in being ruled?'
'Yes, exactly that, and nothing else.'
'Then are you still looking for justice to be something other than this power that produces such men and such cities?'
'No, by Zeus, I'm not,' he said.

'So our dream has come true. The hunch we had at the very start of building the city, that by some god's help we'd hit from the beginning on a kind of origin and pattern of justice, has now been borne out.'
'It certainly has.'
'So the principle that the carpenter and the shoemaker and the rest should each do their own work and not another's, that was a kind of image of justice, which is why it was useful.'
'Plainly.'

'But in truth justice was something of this sort, only it isn't concerned with a man's outward doings but with what's inside him, with his true self and what truly belongs to him. The just man doesn't let any part of his soul do another part's work, or meddle with the others. He sets his own house in order, takes command of himself, brings himself into tune, and becomes a friend to himself. He binds together the three parts, like the three fixed notes of a scale, the highest and the lowest and the one between, and any others there may be in between those, and from being many he becomes entirely one, temperate and in harmony. Only then does he act, whether in getting and spending, or in caring for his body, or in some matter of politics or private dealing, and through it all he believes and calls just and fine any action that preserves this inner harmony and helps produce it, and the knowledge that oversees such action he calls wisdom. And he calls unjust any action that breaks this harmony down, and the belief that oversees that, ignorance.'
'That is the exact truth, Socrates,' he said.
'Good,' I said. 'So if we claimed to have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in each, I don't think we'd be lying.'
'We certainly wouldn't.'
'Shall we say it, then?'
'Let's say it.'
'So be it,' I said. 'And now we have to look at injustice.'
'Plainly.'

'Won't it have to be a kind of civil war among the three parts, a meddling and interfering in one another's work, a rising up of one part of the soul against the whole to seize a rule that isn't its by right, the rule of a part whose nature is to be a subject of the part that ought to rule? Disorder and confusion of that kind, I think, is what we'll call injustice, along with license and cowardice and ignorance, in a word, every form of vice.'
'Exactly so,' he said.
'Then if we know clearly what injustice and justice are, we also know clearly, don't we, what acting unjustly and being unjust come to, and likewise acting justly?'
'How do you mean?' he said.
'They're just like the healthy and the unhealthy,' I said. 'What health and disease are in the body, justice and injustice are in the soul.'
'How so?' he said.
'Healthy things produce health, and unhealthy things produce disease.'
'Yes.'
'And just actions produce justice, unjust actions injustice?'
'They must.'

'And producing health means setting up among the parts of the body a natural order, in which one rules and another is ruled, while producing disease means setting up an order against nature, in which one part rules and another is ruled contrary to nature?'
'True.'
'And isn't producing justice the same, setting up among the parts of the soul a natural order of ruling and being ruled, while producing injustice means an order against nature?'
'Exactly so,' he said.
'So virtue, it seems, is a kind of health and beauty and good condition of the soul, and vice a disease and ugliness and weakness of it.'
'That's right.'
'And don't fine practices lead to virtue, and shameful ones to vice?'
'They must.'

'So now, it seems, all that's left is to ask which pays better, to do what's just, to follow fine practices and be just, whether anyone notices or not, or to do what's unjust and be unjust, provided one isn't punished and so forced to improve.'

'But Socrates,' he said, 'to me that question has become ridiculous. When the body's nature is ruined, we think life isn't worth living, even with all the food and drink and wealth and power in the world. So when the very nature of the thing by which we live is disordered and ruined, are we really going to say life is worth living, as long as a man can do whatever he likes, except the one thing that would free him from vice and injustice and win him justice and virtue, now that we've seen what each of them is?'
'Yes, the question is ridiculous,' I said. 'But still, now that we've come to the point where we can see the truth of all this as clearly as anything, we mustn't give up.'
'No,' he said, 'least of all now.'
'Then come up here,' I said, 'and look down at how many forms vice has, the ones worth looking at, at any rate.'
'I'm right behind you,' he said. 'Go on.'

'From the height the argument has climbed to,' I said, 'it's like standing on a watchtower. From here you can see that virtue is one, but the forms of vice are countless, though four of them are worth singling out.'
'What do you mean?' he said.
'I mean,' I said, 'that there seem to be as many types of soul as there are distinct types of city worth naming.'
'How many is that?'
'Five kinds of city,' I said, 'and five of soul.'
'And what are they?' he asked.

'The first kind of city,' I said, 'is the one we've been describing, and it could go by either of two names. Where one outstanding man rules, you'd call it a monarchy; where several rule, an aristocracy.'
'True,' he said.
'But I count these as a single form. Whether the rulers are one or many, as long as they've been brought up and educated the way we've laid down, they won't disturb the city's fundamental laws.'
'No, they won't,' he said.
